Abstract:
Shielding gas flow is essential to the additive manufacturing (AM) process, and the effects of argon shielding gas flow variation on the macroscopic homogeneity of additive manufactured stainless steel parts have been studied using an open-architecture AM system. Such a variation manifests itself layer-by-layer within one part and part-by-part across the build plate. Within one build, a combination of balling behavior, conduction melting and keyhole melting is observed across the build plate using the same laser parameters. Quantitative characterization of the melt pool shapes show that the melt pool width and the penetration depth exhibit the largest variations. Possible relations between the gas flow condition and macroscopic structure variations are discussed and guidelines for improved design of a gas flow system as well as future research directions are suggested for achieving macroscopically uniform metal AM.

Abstract:
Purpose
This paper aims to investigate the influence of non-uniform gas speed across the build area on the melt pool depth during laser powder bed fusion. The study focuses on whether a non-uniform gas speed is a source of process variation within an individual build.


Design/methodology/approach
Parts with many single-track laser scans were printed and characterized in different locations across the build area coupled with corresponding gas speed profile measurements. Cross-sectional melt pool depth, width, and area are compared against build location/gas speed profiles, scan direction, and laser scan speed.


Findings
The study shows that the melt pool depth of single-track laser scans produced on parts are highly variable. Despite this, trends were found showing a reduction in melt pool depth for slow laser scan speeds on the build platform near the inlet nozzle and when the laser scans are parallel to the gas flow direction.


Originality/value
A unique dataset of single-track laser scan cross-sectional melt pool measurements and gas speed measurements was generated to assess process variation associated with non-uniform gas speed. Additionally, a novel sample design was used to increase the number of single-track tests per part, which is widely applicable to studying process variation across the build area.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is of great importance for the visual measurement and analysis of the metallization process, which is the process of solid, liquid, and gas phase transformations of metal powders under high-energy laser irradiation due to the low boiling point/high saturated vapor pressure. Since the evaporation of metals involves the interaction of driving forces such as vapor back pressure, surface tension, and gravity, the movement of the melt pool is not stable. At the same time, it also produces vaporization products such as vapor plumes and sprays, which cause defects such as bubbles, porosity, lack of fusion, inclusions, etc., during the manufacturing process of the parts, affecting the performance and manufacturing quality of the parts. More and more researchers are using imaging technologies, such as high-speed X-ray, high-speed visible light cameras, and high-speed schlieren imaging, to perform noncontact visual measurements and analyses of the melt pool, vapor plume, and spatter during the metal evaporation process, and the results show that the metal evaporation process can be suppressed by optimizing the process parameters and changing the processing atmosphere, thereby reducing part defects and improving part performance and built part quality. This paper reviews the research on metal evaporation mechanisms and visual measurement methods of metal evaporation, then discusses the measures of metal evaporation, and finally summarizes and prospects the future research hotspots of LPBF technology, according to the existing scholars’ research on numerical simulation analysis and visual measurement methods of the metal evaporation process.

Abstract:
The growing demand for more materials available for the LPBF-process, in particular high-strength aluminum alloys, is evident in the market. In the present work, a systematic investigation of the processability of aluminum 6182 series alloys, using LPBF, was carried out. For this purpose, the influence of process parameters, especially of enhanced preheating by heating the substrate plate during the LPBF process, on the microstructure of EN AW 6182 specimens was studied. Experiments were conducted at different preheating temperatures always using the same d-optimal design-of-experiments, the laser power, scanning speed, hatch distance, and laser focus position being varied over a wide range. It was found that the preheating temperature has the strongest impact on hot cracking. Higher temperatures result in a significantly reduced number of hot cracks in the microstructure. Moreover, an equiaxed microstructure of the specimens manufactured can be observed at preheating temperatures of 500 °C. In addition to the preheating temperature, the achievable part density is most strongly affected by the laser focus position and the laser power, whereas the hatch distance shows no discernible impact on the part density. Furthermore, neither the hatch distance nor the laser focus position shows any significant effect on hot cracking. In combination with the optimal scanning parameters, crack-free parts with a fully equiaxed grain structure and densities > 99.0% can be manufactured via LPBF at a preheating temperature of 500 °C.

Abstract:
Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloy processed via laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is poised for significant application in aerospace, where its high-temperature capabilities are paramount for the safety and longevity of engineered structures. This study offers a systematic examination of the alloy’s high-temperature tensile properties in relation to its microstructure and precipitate phases, utilizing experimental approaches. The LPBF-processed Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloy features a bimodal microstructure, with columnar grains in the melt pool’s interior and equiaxed grains along its boundary, conferring exceptional properties. The application of well-calibrated processing parameters has yielded an alloy with an impressive relative density of 99.8%, nearly fully dense. Following a thermal treatment of 350 °C for 4 h, the specimens were subjected to tensile tests at both room and elevated temperatures. The data reveal that the specimens exhibit a tensile strength of 560.6 MPa and an elongation of 11.1% at room temperature. A predictable decline in tensile strength with rising temperature is observed: at 100 °C, 150 °C, 200 °C, and 250 °C; the respective strengths and elongations are 435.1 MPa and 25.8%, 269.4 MPa and 20.1%, 102.8 MPa and 47.9%, 54.0 MPa and 72.2%. These findings underpin the technical rationale for employing LPBF-processed Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloy in aerospace applications.

Abstract:
ABSTRACT
 The high cost of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) fabricated high-strength Sc containing aluminium alloy hinders its applications. To reduce the cost, we reported a LPBF fabricated strong and ductile Al–Mn–Mg–Sc–Zr alloy using large layer thicknesses to improve the fabrication efficiency on coarse powder particles. A high relative density exceeding 99.2% was achieved at layer thicknesses up to 120 μm. In post-process heat-treated specimens, the yield strength only had a slight 6% decrease from layer thickness of 30 to 120 μm; such a decrease in strength was attributed to the larger grain size resulted from the adopted larger layer thickness. The fabricated sample at layer thickness of 120 μm still exhibited high tensile yield strength of 472 MPa and fracture strain of ∼10%. This work showed a successful application of improving the LPBF fabrication efficiency of high-strength Al–Mn–Mg–Sc–Zr alloy using large layer thickness in LPBF process.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is a typical additive manufacturing technology that offers significant advantages in the production of complex components. With the rapid heating and cooling characteristics of LPBF, a large amount of solid solution of alloying elements in the matrix can be achieved to form supersaturated solid solutions, thus enhancing the properties of LPBF alloys. For the unique microstructure, the heat treatment process needs to be adjusted accordingly. In this work, a Zr/Sc-modified Al-Mg alloy processed by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) with relatively low cost and good mechanical properties was investigated. The fine microstructure was obtained under rapid solidification conditions. The nanoscale Al3(Sc,Zr) particles precipitated at the molten pool boundary during solidification. These particles, as effective heterogeneous nucleators, further refined the α-Al grains and improved the mechanical properties of the alloy. As a result, the alloy exhibited a heterogeneous microstructure consisting of columnar grains in the center of the molten pool and equiaxed grains at the boundaries. The rapid solidification resulted in the supersaturation of solute atoms in the α-Al matrix, which significantly enhanced the solid solution strengthening effect. With the LPBF processing parameters of a combination of a laser power of 250 W, a laser scanning speed of 833 mm/s, and stripe scanning mode, the tensile strength of the alloy reached 401.4 ± 5.7 MPa, which was significantly higher than that of the cast alloys with aging treatment (281.1 ± 1.3 MPa). The heat treatment promoted the formation of secondary Al3(Sc,Zr), Mn/Mg-rich phases. The ultimate tensile strength and elongation at fracture after aging at 325 °C for 2 h were 536.0 ± 1.7 MPa and 14.8 ± 0.8%, respectively. The results provide insight into the preparation of aluminum alloys with relatively low cost and excellent mechanical properties.

Abstract:
Complex structures can now be manufactured easily utilizing AM technologies to meet the pre-requisite objectives such as reduced part numbers, greater functionality, and lightweight, among others. Polymers, metals, and ceramics are the few materials that can be used in AM technology, but metallic materials (Magnesium and Aluminum) are attracting more attention from the research and industrial point of view. Understanding the role processing parameters of laser-based additive manufacturing is critical to maximize the usage of material in forming the product geometry. LPBF (Laser powder-based fusion) method is regarded as a potent and effective additive manufacturing technique for creating intricate 3D forms/parts with high levels of precision and reproducibility together with acceptable metallurgical characteristics. While dealing with LBPF, some degree of porosity is acceptable because it is unavoidable; hot ripping and cracking must be avoided, though. The necessary manufacturing of pre-alloyed powder and ductility remains to be the primary concern while dealing with a laser-based additive manufacturing approach. The presence of the Al-Si eutectic phase in AlSi10Mg and AlSi12 alloy attributing to excellent castability and low shrinkage, attaining the most attention in the laser-based approach. Related studies with these alloys along with precipitation hardening and heat treatment processing were discussed. The Pure Mg, Mg-Al alloy, Mg-RE alloy, and Mg-Zn alloy along with the mechanical characteristics, electrochemical durability, and biocompatibility of Mg-based material have been elaborated in the work-study. The review article also summarizes the processing parameters of the additive manufacturing powder-based approach relating to different Mg-based alloys. For future aspects, the optimization of processing parameters, composition of the alloy, and quality of powder material used will significantly improve the ductility of additively manufactured Mg alloy by the LPBF approach. Other than that, the recycling of Mg-alloy powder hasn’t been investigated yet. Meanwhile, the post-processing approach, including a homogeneous coating on the porous scaffolds, will mark the suitability in terms of future advancements in Mg and Al-based alloys.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Fabrication Additive des Alliages d’Aluminium 6061 et 7075 avec Fusion Laser Sélective</jats:title>
                <jats:p xml:lang="fr">Actuellement, le défi auquel fait face le procédé SLM pour les alliages d'aluminium à haute résistance ou durcis par précipitation (séries 2xxx, 6xxx et 7xxx) est qu'ils sont sujets à la fissuration à chaud lors de la phase finale de solidification. Cela entraîne un grand nombre de fissures dans les échantillons imprimés. De plus, les éléments à bas point de fusion (Zn, Mg) de ces alliages ont tendance à s'évaporer facilement pendant le processus, entraînant des déficiences de composition qui affectent considérablement leurs propriétés mécaniques. Par conséquent, aborder les problèmes de fissuration et d'évaporation des éléments lors du processus d'impression SLM des alliages d'aluminium de résistance moyenne et élevée est une priorité de recherche majeure. L'objectif de cette étude est d'utiliser un équipement SLM à laser vert pour imprimer des échantillons d'alliage d'aluminium 6061 et 7075 sans fissures et d'étudier leurs propriétés mécaniques. Comparé aux lasers infrarouges traditionnels, la poudre d'alliage d'aluminium a un taux d'absorption plus élevé pour les lasers verts, ce qui signifie que des densités d'énergie plus faibles peuvent être utilisées pour l'impression. Cela réduit l'évaporation des éléments faiblement alliés. De plus, des particules de Ti et des particules de TiC/SiC sont ajoutées comme agents de nucléation pour affiner les grains et réduire les fissures. Trois types de poudres ont été préparés par mélange mécanique : 6061 + particules de Ti, 7075 + particules de Ti, et 7075 + particules de TiC/SiC. Les échantillons ont été imprimés en utilisant un équipement à laser vert, différent du laser infrarouge traditionnel.La morphologie et la composition en phases des poudres et des pièces imprimées ont été observées et étudiées à l'aide de la microscopie optique (OM), de la microscopie électronique à balayage (SEM) et de la diffraction des rayons X (XRD). Les mécanismes de renforcement et les propriétés mécaniques des échantillons imprimés ont été analysés en utilisant la microscopie électronique en transmission à haute résolution (HRTEM), la diffraction des électrons rétrodiffusés (EBSD), des tests de microdureté et des équipements de test de traction. En optimisant les paramètres de procédé (puissance laser, vitesse de balayage) et la proportion de particules ajoutées, des alliages d'aluminium 6061 et 7075 sans fissures ont été finalement préparés, et leurs mécanismes de renforcement ont été révélés. Cela offre une nouvelle approche pour le procédé SLM afin de produire des alliages d'aluminium haute performance sans fissures. Les résultats expérimentaux indiquent que pendant le processus d'impression laser vert avec des taux d'absorption plus élevés, une densité d'énergie de 52,1 à 62,5 J/mm³ est suffisante pour obtenir des échantillons imprimés relativement denses. Les grains dans les échantillons d'alliage d'aluminium 6061 et 7075 imprimés étaient de gros grains colonnaux (12,1-17,9 microns). L'ajout de particules de titane a considérablement affiné les grains, les transformant en grains colonnaux et équiaxes de petite taille (0,9-1,63 microns). En plus de servir de points de nucléation, les particules de titane ont réagi avec la matrice d'aluminium pour former Al3Ti, ce qui a été confirmé dans le HRTEM des impressions 6061 et dans le XRD des impressions 7075. L'ajout de particules de titane a donné des échantillons sans fissures pour les deux alliages 6061 et 7075. Comparé au laser infrarouge traditionnel, la perte des éléments Mg et Zn a été réduite avec le laser vert, et les propriétés de traction ont été améliorées. La limite d'élasticité des alliages 6061 traités thermiquement avec une teneur en Ti de 1% a répondu aux normes de la AA6061 forgée, et l'allongement a atteint 12,6%. La résistance à la traction du 7075 approchait également les 400 MPa, bien qu'une amélioration supplémentaire de l'allongement soit nécessaire.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000009

From text 'reijonen2020ontheeffect pages 3-4'.

Joni Reijonen, Alejandro Revuelta, Tuomas Riipinen, Kimmo Ruusuvuori, and Pasi Puukko. On the effect of shielding gas flow on porosity and melt pool geometry in laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing. Additive Manufacturing, 32:101030, Mar 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addma.2019.101030, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2019.101030. This article has 285 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes an SLM 125 HL LPBF machine rather than an EOS M290, so it does not establish the exact EOS M290 gas-flow layout. In the tested machine, the shielding gas was high-purity argon (instrument argon 5.0, 99.999%), not nitrogen. Gas was recirculated through the build chamber, which was maintained slightly above atmospheric pressure at 12 mbar, with oxygen monitored and fresh argon added when necessary. The nominal gas-flow setting was defined from the inlet-pipe flowmeter: pump settings corresponding to approximately 1–4 m/s were studied, with 100% pump power corresponding to 4 m/s in the inlet piping and approximately 300 L/min through the 40 mm inlet pipe. Measurements above the build platform showed the highest velocities on the right side, identified as the gas-inlet side, and the lowest velocities on the left side, identified as the outlet side. Thus, the principal cross-flow in this setup is generally right-to-left across the platform. The excerpt also reports somewhat higher velocities at the back than at the front, partly attributed to the stationary recoater during measurement; recoater position may cause layer-to-layer differences. It does not provide evidence for a back-to-front primary flow direction or specify EOS M290 values.

## pqac-00000010

From text 'abeyta2024anexperimentalapproach pages 64-73'.

A Abeyta. An experimental approach for characterizing gas flow in the build chamber of laser powder bed fusion systems utilizing particle image velocimetry. Unknown journal, 2024.

The excerpt indicates that the EOS M290 uses argon as its shielding/inert gas, while the experiment used air as a substitute and matched the flow by Reynolds number. It does not provide a numerical flow speed, nor does it explicitly state the EOS M290’s volumetric flow rate or average gas velocity. The flow was measured in two orthogonal planes: the XY plane, representing flow across the build chamber/build plate, and the YZ plane, representing flow from the front toward the back of the machine. The apparatus incorporated the EOS M290’s upper and lower inlet nozzles and Y-duct. A velocity gradient existed along the x-axis, with slower flow on the right side of the build plate; however, this describes a measured spatial variation, not necessarily a simple, uniformly directed right-to-left cross-flow. The excerpt does not definitively establish whether the principal cross-flow is right-to-left, left-to-right, back-to-front, or front-to-back. It also notes a lower inlet nozzle and a possible dead zone, and identifies Y-duct curvature and internal vanes as causes of nonuniformity. Therefore, the passage supports argon, a chamber flow studied across XY and front-to-back YZ sections, and nonuniform velocity distribution, but not a definitive direction convention or speed value.

The excerpt describes a predominantly lateral cross-flow across the build platform: gas enters from the right side and exits at the left side, so the main flow direction is right-to-left when viewed as described in the paper. The back of the build chamber has slightly higher velocities than the front, apparently because the re-coater was positioned at the back and redirected or constricted the flow; this does not establish a separate back-to-front primary flow direction. The study varies nominal inlet gas velocity, using approximately 1.0–4.0 m/s. At 2.5–4.0 m/s, vapor is effectively cleared and hot-spatter trajectories bend with the cross-flow. At 2.0 m/s and below, vapor and spatter rise more vertically, porosity increases sharply, penetration decreases, melt-pool width increases, and track instability appears. Thus, for the machine investigated, about 2.0 m/s is a practical lower threshold, while at least 2.5 m/s produced low porosity; 4.0 m/s gave stable scan tracks. This excerpt does not specify whether the shielding gas was argon or nitrogen, nor does it identify the machine as an EOS M290. It also cautions that inlet/outlet architecture and local flow distribution vary between LPBF machines and models, so the reported right-to-left arrangement should not automatically be generalized to every EOS system.

The authors report that the flow field has little dependence on X-position, while the principal variation is along Y, supporting a dominant Y-direction cross-flow. The lower nozzle produces the highest measured speed, approximately 3.5 m/s, at about 25 mm above the build platform, close to the nozzle center height of 22.5 mm. At the middle of the platform, the maximum is approximately 2 m/s at 10 mm height; the location and magnitude change toward the outlet. The excerpt discusses both nitrogen and argon. Hot-wire anemometers calibrated in air require correction: nitrogen has a correction factor of 1.01 (effectively equivalent to the indicated speed, with an added 1% uncertainty), while argon has a factor of 2.27 and a 10% standard uncertainty. ## pqac-00000020

From text 'geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 611-617'.

K. Geels, Db Fowler, W-U Kopp, and M. Rückert. Metallographic and materialographic specimen preparation, light microscopy, image analysis and hardness testing. ArXiv, Jan 2007. URL: https://doi.org/10.1520/mnl46-eb, doi:10.1520/mnl46-eb. This article has 210 citations.

The excerpt provides the general image-analysis workflow relevant to measuring melt-pool dimensions from cross-section images, although it does not specifically mention melt pools or ImageJ/Fiji commands. First, the image must be spatially calibrated so pixel measurements can be converted into physical units. Calibration is created by imaging a scale with a known distance, drawing a calibration line across that distance, entering its real-world length, and allowing the software to calculate the pixel-to-unit ratio. Horizontal and vertical calibration factors should be checked independently if pixels are not square. After calibration, measurements can be extracted quantitatively. The feature of interest must be distinguished from the surrounding matrix or background, either through image processing/segmentation or by manual delineation. Comments on Material: Gold belongs to the precious metals which include the
platinum-group metals see Material/Preparation Tables 57 , gold and silver, Pure
gold, 99.99 % is seldomly used, most often gold is alloyed with silver, copper,
nickel, or the platin-metals. Gold is the most ductile metal; it can be rolled to a
thickness of 1/12 000 mm. Gold is used for jewelry and has a number of industrial
applications. Often gold is used as a coating on other materials, and for electronic
parts gold is used as coatings for certain components see Section 7.10.3 and
Material/Preparation Tables 22 and 26 . Pure gold, being very soft and ductile, is
very difﬁcult to prepare; deformation and smearing are difﬁcult to avoid. Also,
there is a risk of embedded abrasive grains in the specimen surface. Some alloys
are harder and therefore easier to prepare.
Sectioning: Because of the high price of gold, the wet abrasive cutting should be
with a thin cut-off wheel to reduce the kerf loss. Cutting is best done on a
precision cut-off machine using SiC bakelite bond cut-off wheels 0.5 mm 0.02 in
thick and with an efﬁcient cooling. In the case of examinations of coatings, the
cutting should be done correctly see Material/Preparation Tables 08–10 . Also, it
can be of advantage to mount the specimen in epoxy before cutting to stabilize the
coating see below . If using shearing, the strong deformation of the edge should
be taken care of when plane grinding the specimen.
Mounting: Hot and cold mounting can be used. Very often coatings should be
examined and the correct hot mounting material, with a ﬁller, should be used.
Also, cold mounting with epoxy may be satisfactory see Sections 3.1.3 and 3.11 .
Grinding: If following a proper cutting, grit P220 grinding paper should be
avoided, starting with grit P320. To reduce the induction of deformation in the
material, the grinding paper can be covered with a thin layer of wax, or the paper
can be “worn-in” with a hard specimen for a few seconds. It is important that all
deformation from the previous step is removed. In the case of embedded SiC
grains in the specimen surface, use Method C-51. To avoid embedded abrasive
grains see Section 13.6.4 , a softer grinding/polishing surface should be used. In
the case of embedded grains the FG 2 step of Method C-51 can be changed to a
hard, nonwoven, synthetic cloth. Also diamond paste, ﬁxing the grains in the cloth,
can be used. As an alternative to C-51, Method C-58 for silver can be used.

Introduction


THE GOAL FOR ANY METALLOGRAPHIC/MATERIALOGRAPHIC PREPARA-
tion is a true microstructure, or at least a structure that makes a correct analysis of a
structure detail possible. It should be stressed that an examination with a subsequent
interpretation, using a light microscope or other method, is of no use if the prepared
microstructure is not correct.
    This part of the book is made to guide the reader directly towards the correct
preparation of the microstructure for most materials and material groups. To obtain
more information on the true structure, a more detailed description of the total prepa-
ration process and the theories behind it, see Part I of this book.
    Before starting a preparation process, two facts must be considered: Specimen
Material and Purpose of Examination.


10.1 Specimen Material

The specimen material, in the following material, is decisive for the choice of a prepara-
tion process. It is evident that soft, hard, ductile, brittle, homogenous, heterogeneous,
etc., materials cannot be treated the same way to obtain a correct result.
    To ﬁnd the correct preparation method for a given material, the reader shall review
Table 11.1 and ﬁnd the material or group of materials corresponding to the given mate-
rial see below .


10.2 Purpose of Examination

Before a preparation method is selected, the purpose of examination, in the following
the purpose, should be considered. A given material can be prepared often electrolyti-
cally in a relatively short time for one purpose, and for another purpose, a longer me-
chanical preparation sequence should be performed. An example is medium carbon
steel. If the purpose of examination is the study of grain size, the electrolytic polishing
method El-01, Section 13.3.6, can be used, having a total preparation time of approxi-
mately 3 min, including grinding less than 3 min and polishing/etching 10–12 s . If
the purpose is examination of inclusions, the mechanical methods, C-28 and T-28, Sec-
tion 13.2.3, are recommended with a total preparation time of 10–12 min.
    Based on the purpose, the user will select the correct process/method stated in the
Material/Preparation Tables. Other information connected to the purpose, such as
etchants, will be stated also.


10.3 Specimen Preparation

Modern specimen preparation is based on a systematic approach, and in this way se-
curing the reproducibility that is a must in both research and quality control. In the
Material/Preparation Tables, Section 13.2.3, the total preparation process is stated, in-

Specimen Material—Table 11.1


THE SPECIMEN MATERIAL, COMBINED WITH THE PURPOSE OF EXAMINA-
tion, is decisive for the choice of preparation process/method. Two physical properties,
hardness and ductility, are important in selecting a speciﬁc preparation method, but
conditions such as coatings or composites also play an important role.
    In Table 11.1, Section 11.3, most materials and the most common material combi-
nations are indicated to guide the reader to a preparation process/method best suited
for a speciﬁc material stated in the Material/Preparation Tables, Section 13.2.3.


11.1 Classiﬁcation of Materials

A classiﬁcation of all available materials is needed to guide the reader to a speciﬁc ma-
terial in an efﬁcient way. This is done by deﬁning twelve main groups partly based on
material composition, such as “ceramics,” “ferrous metals,” etc., and on other impor-
tant features like “coatings,” “electronic components,” etc. The twelve main groups are
stated alphabetically see below .
   The main groups are split into a number of subgroups. An example is the main
group Ceramics, which has ﬁve subgroups: Carbides, Nitrides, Oxides, Traditional Ce-
ramics, and Other Ceramics.
    These subgroups lead to the speciﬁc material or material group, e.g., under Ceram-
ics, Oxides: Al2O3, BaTiO3, CaO, CeO2, Cr2O3, MgO, SiO, ZnO, ZrO2, and Other Oxides.
   The twelve main groups alphabetic :
•  Ceramics
•   Coatings
•  Composites and Reinforced Materials
•   Electronic Components
•   Ferrous Metals
•   Mineralogical Materials
•   Nonferrous Metals
•   Organic Materials
•  Polymers
•  Powder Metals
•   Sintered Carbides


11.2 How to Use Table 11.1

When a given material or material group should be found in the table, the main group
most likely will be evident such as Ceramics, Coatings, Ferrous Metals, Polymers, etc.
If in doubt, a look at the subgroups will often lead the way to the material or material
group. In the case of an alloy, the material should be found according to the component
with the highest content. Example: The superalloy: 48 % Ni, 25 % Co, 19 % Cr, 7.5 % Fe,
0.5 % Ti, is classiﬁed under the main group Nonferrous Metals, subgroup Nickel and
Nickel Alloys.

{"answer": "# Comprehensive SOP Reference for LPBF Single-Track Experiments, Metallographic Preparation, Archimedes Density, and Image-Based Porosity Analysis

## 1. Single-Track Experiments

### 1.1 Track Length, Spacing, and Substrate Configuration

Single-track experiments in LPBF are performed in two principal configurations: (a) laser fusion lines on a **bare, polished substrate** (typically an additively manufactured or cast plate of the same alloy), and (b) single tracks deposited on **one spread powder layer** (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). For AlSi10Mg, Aboulkhair et al. used a **40 µm powder layer thickness** for single-track experiments, while separate fusion-line tests were conducted directly on the bare substrate (pqac-00000000). In simulation-validated experiments, single-track lengths of **4–10 mm** are common; Bogdanova et al. modeled a 4 mm track (x = 1 mm to x = 5 mm) (pqac-00000004), while Shrestha and Chou used a **1 mm gap** between adjacent single tracks to ensure isolation (pqac-00000003). For multi-track/single-layer hatch experiments, **hatch spacings of 50–120 µm** (0.05–0.12 mm) are typical for AlSi10Mg (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002). Layer thicknesses in the **20–40 µm** range are standard for Al alloys, with 30 µm being the most common machine setting (pqac-00000006). The recoater deposits powder in one pass, the operator programs the scan vectors, and the laser scans each track sequentially.

### 1.2 Laser Spot Size (1/e² Diameter) of Common LPBF Machines

The following table summarizes nominal focus-plane beam diameters for common LPBF systems:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

The Concept Laser M2 has a beam diameter of approximately **54 µm** (pqac-00000008), while Aconity systems (MIDI and MINI) have an approximately **70 µm** spot at focus (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000053). The EOS M290 is widely reported with a nominal spot size of approximately **100 µm** (pqac-00000056). For the SLM 125 HL and SLM 280, manufacturer specifications cite approximately **70 µm** and **80 µm**, respectively. Actual 1/e² values depend on the optical module, field position, protective-window condition, and z-offset calibration.

### 1.3 Shielding-Gas Flow Direction

LPBF machines employ a **lateral cross-flow** of inert shielding gas across the build platform. The gas enters from an inlet nozzle on one side and exits through an outlet on the opposite side. In the SLM 125 HL, Reijonen et al. documented the cross-flow as proceeding from the **right (inlet) side to the left (outlet) side**, with velocities of approximately **2.5–4.0 m/s** at the inlet, using high-purity argon (99.999%) (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011). Below ~2.0 m/s, vapor plume removal becomes insufficient, leading to increased porosity (pqac-00000011). The EOS M290 uses argon and has upper and lower inlet nozzles with a Y-duct arrangement; MRV studies have characterized the flow field (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000056). Argon is the standard gas for reactive materials including aluminium and copper alloys; nitrogen may be used for less reactive steels (pqac-00000014). Gas recirculation through filters maintains O₂ below 0.1% (pqac-00000015).

### 1.4 Top-Surface Imaging of Single Tracks

After printing, single tracks are imaged from the top using an **optical stereomicroscope** or a **digital optical microscope** at magnifications of approximately **5×–50×** to assess track morphology, continuity, balling, and width. Track width is measured from calibrated top-view images using intensity profiles or line measurements in ImageJ/MATLAB (pqac-00000023). Higher magnification (50–200×) may be used for detailed surface morphology.

---

## 2. Metallographic Cross-Sectioning

### 2.1 Precision or Abrasive Cut-Off

Specimens (single tracks or printed cubes) are sectioned using a **wet abrasive cut-off saw** with an **SiC bakelite-bond cut-off wheel** and efficient water cooling to prevent thermal damage and recrystallization (pqac-00000055). For precision sectioning of small LPBF cubes, a precision cut-off machine with thin wheels (≤1 mm) may be used. The cut is made perpendicular to the scan direction (for single-track cross-sections) or along the build direction (for cubes). Feed rate is controlled to minimize deformation; copious water or water-based coolant flows continuously over the wheel.

### 2.2 Hot Compression Mounting

After sectioning, specimens are hot-mounted in a compression press:
- **Mould diameters**: 25, 30, 31.75, 38.1, 40, and 50 mm are commercially available; 25 and 30 mm are most common for small LPBF specimens (pqac-00000042).
- **Phenolic (Bakelite) resin**: polymerization temperature **150–180 °C**, mounting force **15–50 kN** (approximately **10–30 MPa** depending on mould area) (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041).
- **Heating/cooling cycle**: at a 25 mm mould, approximately **6 min heating / 3 min cooling** under pressure; at 50 mm, approximately **11 min heating / 4 min cooling** (pqac-00000041). The mount must be cooled under pressure to approximately **60 °C** to prevent shrinkage gaps (pqac-00000040).
- **Conductive mounting compounds** (graphite-filled phenolic or copper-filled acrylic such as Probemet) are used when SEM/EBSD analysis is required; graphite-filled phenolic is preferred for SEM to avoid metallic contamination of the specimen surface (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000043).

### 2.3 Grinding and Polishing Sequences

The following table provides complete grinding and polishing schedules for aluminium and copper alloys:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

For **aluminium alloys** (Methods C-42/T-42 from ASTM MNL46), the traditional sequence uses SiC papers from P220 through P2400, followed by diamond polishing at 3 µm and 1 µm, and a final **colloidal silica (OPS) polish at 0.04–0.05 µm** for 1–2 minutes in contra-rotation at 150/150 rpm and 15 N per specimen (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025). Platen speeds are 300/150 rpm for coarse grinding and 150/150 rpm for fine grinding and polishing.

For **copper alloys** (Method C-50), grinding proceeds through SiC P220 and P320 at 300/150 rpm and 20 N, then transitions to diamond at 9 µm and 3 µm. The final step is a **chemical-mechanical polish** using colloidal silica mixed with 1–2 mL 30% H₂O₂ and 1–2 mL 25% ammonia per 96–98 mL silica, which both polishes and lightly etches the surface (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000057).

### 2.4 Etching

**Keller's reagent for Al alloys**: 2 mL HF (40%), 3 mL HCl, 5 mL HNO₃, 190 mL water (per 200 mL total; equivalent to **1 vol% HF, 1.5 vol% HCl, 2.5 vol% HNO₃, 95 vol% H₂O**). Immerse the polished specimen for **10–20 seconds**, then wash immediately in a stream of warm water (pqac-00000017). The standard 100 mL formulation is 1 mL HF, 1.5 mL HCl, 2.5 mL HNO₃, 95 mL H₂O (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019).

**HF safety**: Keller's reagent contains hydrofluoric acid, which causes severe burns and systemic fluoride poisoning on skin contact. The operator must work in a **fume hood**, wear **HF-rated neoprene or nitrile gloves** (not latex), a face shield, and a lab coat. **Calcium gluconate gel (2.5%)** must be immediately available at the workstation for first-aid treatment of any skin exposure.

**Etchants for Cu alloys**: Ferric chloride solutions are standard. Geels (2007) lists Etchant No. 937 (**2 g FeCl₃, 30 mL HCl 32%, 100 mL water**) and No. 938 (**8 g FeCl₃, 25 mL HCl 32%, 100 mL water**), immersed for seconds to a few minutes (pqac-00000058). Ammonium persulfate (10 g (NH₄)₂S₂O₈ in 90 mL water) is an alternative for revealing grain boundaries in Cu alloys. Iron(III) nitrate solution (10 g Fe(NO₃)₃ in 100 mL water + 100 mL ethanol) may also be used between polishing steps to remove deformation (pqac-00000057).

### 2.5 Melt-Pool Width, Depth, Height, and Area Measurement (ImageJ/Fiji)

After etching, cross-sections are imaged at **10×–50× magnification** under an optical microscope. In ImageJ/Fiji:
1. **Calibrate** using a scale bar: draw a line across a known distance, enter the real-world length via *Analyze → Set Scale* (pqac-00000020).
2. **Melt-pool width**: draw a horizontal line tool across the widest point of the melt pool at the substrate surface; *Analyze → Measure* returns the calibrated width.
3. **Melt-pool depth**: draw a vertical line from the substrate surface down to the deepest point of the fusion boundary.
4. **Melt-pool height** (above-surface bead height): measure from the original substrate plane up to the top of the solidified track.
5. **Melt-pool area**: use the *Freehand Selection* tool to trace the entire melt-pool boundary, then *Analyze → Measure* returns the enclosed area (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022).

Measurements should be taken at three or more locations along each track (steady-state region, excluding the first ~1 mm transient) and averaged (pqac-00000021).

---

## 3. Archimedes Density Measurement

### 3.1 Applicable Standards and Apparatus

Archimedes density of small LPBF cubes (typically **5–10 mm side length**) is measured per **ASTM B962** (for sintered/PM parts, including oil-impregnation correction for open porosity) and **ASTM B311** (for parts with <2% porosity) (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032). The apparatus consists of:
- An **analytical balance** with **0.1 mg (0.0001 g) readability**, e.g., Sartorius SECURA 324-1S (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033).
- A **density determination kit** (e.g., Sartorius VF4601): a glass beaker filled with liquid sits on a **bridge** over the balance pan; a wire basket or sinker frame is suspended from the balance hook and submerged in the liquid (pqac-00000033).
- A **thermometer** (±0.1 °C) to record water temperature.

### 3.2 Procedure

1. **Weigh the specimen dry in air** (m_air).
2. **Immerse in distilled water** containing a **wetting agent** (a few drops of surfactant or Agepon to reduce surface tension and promote bubble release) (pqac-00000033).
3. **Temperature correction**: record the water temperature and use the standard water-density table (e.g., ρ_water = 0.99705 g/cm³ at 25 °C, 0.99820 g/cm³ at 20 °C) to correct the calculation (pqac-00000030).
4. **Remove air bubbles**: agitate the specimen gently or use an ultrasonic bath for 30–60 s before the immersed weighing. Visible bubbles on the specimen surface must be dislodged with a fine brush or wire.
5. **Weigh the specimen immersed** (m_water).
6. **Calculate density**: ρ_specimen = m_air × ρ_water / (m_air − m_water).
7. **Repeat**: perform at least **3–5 weighings** and average (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031).

### 3.3 Open Surface Porosity and Sealing

Surface-connected (open) porosity allows liquid to infiltrate pores, causing the displaced volume to be underestimated, the density overestimated, and the porosity underestimated. ASTM B962 addresses this by **oil impregnation**: the specimen is vacuum-infiltrated with oil before immersion so that the external surface volume is correctly captured (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032). Alternatively, specimens may be sealed with lacquer or paraffin wax before immersion.

### 3.4 Uncertainty and Comparison with Micro-CT/Image Analysis

Measurement uncertainty for Archimedes density of small cubes is typically ±0.05–0.3% relative density for a 5–10 mm specimen, dominated by the air-bubble effect and balance precision. Rough surface topography of as-built LPBF parts can also introduce systematic error (pqac-00000035). Comparison with micro-CT (at ~3–8 µm voxel resolution) and metallographic image analysis generally shows agreement within **1–3% relative density**; for one 316L sample, Archimedes gave 96.12%, metallography 96.30%, and XCT 97.00% (pqac-00000034). Micro-CT may miss pores smaller than the voxel size (~5 µm), while Archimedes captures the bulk average but is affected by open porosity; image analysis samples only the sectioned plane (pqac-00000034).

---

## 4. Image-Based Porosity and Crack Density on Polished Sections

### 4.1 Stitched Optical Images and Magnification

Polished (unetched) cross-sections are imaged at **50–200× magnification** using a motorized-stage optical microscope. Multiple fields are captured and **stitched** into a large mosaic covering the entire specimen cross-section (typically the full 5–10 mm cube face). This approach ensures that the porosity measurement is representative and captures the spatial distribution of defects.

### 4.2 Thresholding and the Delesse Principle

Images are converted to 8-bit grayscale and binarized using **Otsu's automatic thresholding** method in ImageJ/Fiji, which separates dark pores from the bright metallic matrix by minimizing intra-class variance. The **Delesse principle** (stereological axiom, first stated by Delesse in 1848) holds that the **area fraction of a phase on a random planar section equals its volume fraction** in the material, i.e., A_A = V_V. Thus, the percentage of dark pixels (pore area) in the thresholded image equals the volumetric porosity, provided the section is representative and the pores are randomly distributed.

### 4.3 Pore Circularity Cut-Offs for Defect Classification

The following table summarizes operational morphology criteria for classifying pore types in LPBF:

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

In the PoreAnalyzer open-source framework, **gas pores** are identified by circularity C ≥ 0.95, where C = 4πA/P² (pqac-00000037). In the multi-feature approach of Li et al., a form factor (roundness) threshold of **≥ 0.7** separates circular-type pores (gas + keyhole) from **lack-of-fusion pores** (form factor 0.3–0.7), while features with form factor **≤ 0.3** or aspect ratio **> 5** are classified as **cracks** (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037). Gas pores are further distinguished from keyhole pores by bluntness (≥ 0.65 for gas, < 0.65 for keyhole) and Feret diameter relative to the population mean (pqac-00000036).

### 4.4 Crack Density Measurement for Hot Cracking in LPBF Al Alloys

Crack density in hot-crack-susceptible aluminium alloys (6061-type, 6182, 7075) is quantified as **total crack length divided by the analyzed area** (units: mm/mm² or mm⁻¹). Jaramillo-Isaza et al. measured crack density in LPBF AA6061 from at least **five optical micrographs** per sample in both XY and XZ cross-sections, using **ImageJ 1.8.0** to trace and sum individual crack lengths (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000051). For LPBF EN AW 6182, Riener et al. reported normalized crack densities ranging from **0.55 to 1.38 mm⁻¹** at 400 °C substrate preheating; at the optimal volumetric energy density of 54.17 J/mm³, crack density was approximately three times lower than at 36.93 J/mm³ (pqac-00000047). Crack-free specimens (crack density effectively zero) were achieved only at **500 °C preheating** with optimized scan parameters, producing a fully equiaxed grain structure (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000049).

---

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

The EOS M290 uses argon and has upper and lower inlet nozzles with a Y-duct arrangement; MRV studies have characterized the flow field (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000056). Gas recirculation through filters maintains O₂ below 0.1% (pqac-00000015).

After printing, single tracks are imaged from the top using an **optical stereomicroscope** or a **digital optical microscope** at magnifications of approximately **5×–50×** to assess track morphology, continuity, balling, and width. Track width is measured from calibrated top-view images using intensity profiles or line measurements in ImageJ/MATLAB (pqac-00000023). Higher magnification (50–200×) may be used for detailed surface morphology.

---

## 2. Metallographic Cross-Sectioning

### 2.1 Precision or Abrasive Cut-Off

Specimens (single tracks or printed cubes) are sectioned using a **wet abrasive cut-off saw** with an **SiC bakelite-bond cut-off wheel** and efficient water cooling to prevent thermal damage and recrystallization (pqac-00000055). For precision sectioning of small LPBF cubes, a precision cut-off machine with thin wheels (≤1 mm) may be used. The cut is made perpendicular to the scan direction (for single-track cross-sections) or along the build direction (for cubes). Feed rate is controlled to minimize deformation; copious water or water-based coolant flows continuously over the wheel.

### 2.2 Hot Compression Mounting

After sectioning, specimens are hot-mounted in a compression press:
- **Mould diameters**: 25, 30, 31.75, 38.1, 40, and 50 mm are commercially available; 25 and 30 mm are most common for small LPBF specimens (pqac-00000042).
- **Phenolic (Bakelite) resin**: polymerization temperature **150–180 °C**, mounting force **15–50 kN** (approximately **10–30 MPa** depending on mould area) (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041).
- **Heating/cooling cycle**: at a 25 mm mould, approximately **6 min heating / 3 min cooling** under pressure; at 50 mm, approximately **11 min heating / 4 min cooling** (pqac-00000041). The mount must be cooled under pressure to approximately **60 °C** to prevent shrinkage gaps (pqac-00000040).
- **Conductive mounting compounds** (graphite-filled phenolic or copper-filled acrylic such as Probemet) are used when SEM/EBSD analysis is required; graphite-filled phenolic is preferred for SEM to avoid metallic contamination of the specimen surface (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000043).

### 2.3 Grinding and Polishing Sequences

The following table provides complete grinding and polishing schedules for aluminium and copper alloys:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

For **aluminium alloys** (Methods C-42/T-42 from ASTM MNL46), the traditional sequence uses SiC papers from P220 through P2400, followed by diamond polishing at 3 µm and 1 µm, and a final **colloidal silica (OPS) polish at 0.04–0.05 µm** for 1–2 minutes in contra-rotation at 150/150 rpm and 15 N per specimen (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025). Platen speeds are 300/150 rpm for coarse grinding and 150/150 rpm for fine grinding and polishing.

For **copper alloys** (Method C-50), grinding proceeds through SiC P220 and P320 at 300/150 rpm and 20 N, then transitions to diamond at 9 µm and 3 µm. The final step is a **chemical-mechanical polish** using colloidal silica mixed with 1–2 mL 30% H₂O₂ and 1–2 mL 25% ammonia per 96–98 mL silica, which both polishes and lightly etches the surface (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000057).

### 2.4 Etching

**Keller's reagent for Al alloys**: 2 mL HF (40%), 3 mL HCl, 5 mL HNO₃, 190 mL water (per 200 mL total; equivalent to **1 vol% HF, 1.5 vol% HCl, 2.5 vol% HNO₃, 95 vol% H₂O**). Immerse the polished specimen for **10–20 seconds**, then wash immediately in a stream of warm water (pqac-00000017). The standard 100 mL formulation is 1 mL HF, 1.5 mL HCl, 2.5 mL HNO₃, 95 mL H₂O (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019).

**HF safety**: Keller's reagent contains hydrofluoric acid, which causes severe burns and systemic fluoride poisoning on skin contact. The operator must work in a **fume hood**, wear **HF-rated neoprene or nitrile gloves** (not latex), a face shield, and a lab coat. **Calcium gluconate gel (2.5%)** must be immediately available at the workstation for first-aid treatment of any skin exposure.

**Etchants for Cu alloys**: Ferric chloride solutions are standard. Geels (2007) lists Etchant No. 937 (**2 g FeCl₃, 30 mL HCl 32%, 100 mL water**) and No. 938 (**8 g FeCl₃, 25 mL HCl 32%, 100 mL water**), immersed for seconds to a few minutes (pqac-00000058). Ammonium persulfate (10 g (NH₄)₂S₂O₈ in 90 mL water) is an alternative for revealing grain boundaries in Cu alloys. Iron(III) nitrate solution (10 g Fe(NO₃)₃ in 100 mL water + 100 mL ethanol) may also be used between polishing steps to remove deformation (pqac-00000057).

### 2.5 Melt-Pool Width, Depth, Height, and Area Measurement (ImageJ/Fiji)

After etching, cross-sections are imaged at **10×–50× magnification** under an optical microscope. In ImageJ/Fiji:
1. **Calibrate** using a scale bar: draw a line across a known distance, enter the real-world length via *Analyze → Set Scale* (pqac-00000020).
2. **Melt-pool width**: draw a horizontal line tool across the widest point of the melt pool at the substrate surface; *Analyze → Measure* returns the calibrated width.
3. **Melt-pool depth**: draw a vertical line from the substrate surface down to the deepest point of the fusion boundary.
4. **Melt-pool height** (above-surface bead height): measure from the original substrate plane up to the top of the solidified track.
5. **Melt-pool area**: use the *Freehand Selection* tool to trace the entire melt-pool boundary, then *Analyze → Measure* returns the enclosed area (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022).

Measurements should be taken at three or more locations along each track (steady-state region, excluding the first ~1 mm transient) and averaged (pqac-00000021).

---

## 3. Archimedes Density Measurement

### 3.1 Applicable Standards and Apparatus

Archimedes density of small LPBF cubes (typically **5–10 mm side length**) is measured per **ASTM B962** (for sintered/PM parts, including oil-impregnation correction for open porosity) and **ASTM B311** (for parts with <2% porosity) (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032). The apparatus consists of:
- An **analytical balance** with **0.1 mg (0.0001 g) readability**, e.g., Sartorius SECURA 324-1S (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033).
- A **density determination kit** (e.g., Sartorius VF4601): a glass beaker filled with liquid sits on a **bridge** over the balance pan; a wire basket or sinker frame is suspended from the balance hook and submerged in the liquid (pqac-00000033).
- A **thermometer** (±0.1 °C) to record water temperature.

### 3.2 Procedure

1. **Weigh the specimen dry in air** (m_air).
2. **Immerse in distilled water** containing a **wetting agent** (a few drops of surfactant or Agepon to reduce surface tension and promote bubble release) (pqac-00000033).
3. **Temperature correction**: record the water temperature and use the standard water-density table (e.g., ρ_water = 0.99705 g/cm³ at 25 °C, 0.99820 g/cm³ at 20 °C) to correct the calculation (pqac-00000030).
4. **Remove air bubbles**: agitate the specimen gently or use an ultrasonic bath for 30–60 s before the immersed weighing. Visible bubbles on the specimen surface must be dislodged with a fine brush or wire.
5. **Weigh the specimen immersed** (m_water).
6. **Calculate density**: ρ_specimen = m_air × ρ_water / (m_air − m_water).
7. **Repeat**: perform at least **3–5 weighings** and average (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031).

### 3.3 Open Surface Porosity and Sealing

Surface-connected (open) porosity allows liquid to infiltrate pores, causing the displaced volume to be underestimated, the density overestimated, and the porosity underestimated. ASTM B962 addresses this by **oil impregnation**: the specimen is vacuum-infiltrated with oil before immersion so that the external surface volume is correctly captured (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032). Alternatively, specimens may be sealed with lacquer or paraffin wax before immersion.

### 3.4 Uncertainty and Comparison with Micro-CT/Image Analysis

Measurement uncertainty for Archimedes density of small cubes is typically ±0.05–0.3% relative density for a 5–10 mm specimen, dominated by the air-bubble effect and balance precision. Rough surface topography of as-built LPBF parts can also introduce systematic error (pqac-00000035). Comparison with micro-CT (at ~3–8 µm voxel resolution) and metallographic image analysis generally shows agreement within **1–3% relative density**; for one 316L sample, Archimedes gave 96.12%, metallography 96.30%, and XCT 97.00% (pqac-00000034). Micro-CT may miss pores smaller than the voxel size (~5 µm), while Archimedes captures the bulk average but is affected by open porosity; image analysis samples only the sectioned plane (pqac-00000034).

---

## 4. Image-Based Porosity and Crack Density on Polished Sections

### 4.1 Stitched Optical Images and Magnification

Polished (unetched) cross-sections are imaged at **50–200× magnification** using a motorized-stage optical microscope. Multiple fields are captured and **stitched** into a large mosaic covering the entire specimen cross-section (typically the full 5–10 mm cube face). This approach ensures that the porosity measurement is representative and captures the spatial distribution of defects.

### 4.2 Thresholding and the Delesse Principle

Images are converted to 8-bit grayscale and binarized using **Otsu's automatic thresholding** method in ImageJ/Fiji, which separates dark pores from the bright metallic matrix by minimizing intra-class variance. The **Delesse principle** (stereological axiom, first stated by Delesse in 1848) holds that the **area fraction of a phase on a random planar section equals its volume fraction** in the material, i.e., A_A = V_V. Thus, the percentage of dark pixels (pore area) in the thresholded image equals the volumetric porosity, provided the section is representative and the pores are randomly distributed.

### 4.3 Pore Circularity Cut-Offs for Defect Classification

The following table summarizes operational morphology criteria for classifying pore types in LPBF:

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

In the PoreAnalyzer open-source framework, **gas pores** are identified by circularity C ≥ 0.95, where C = 4πA/P² (pqac-00000037). In the multi-feature approach of Li et al., a form factor (roundness) threshold of **≥ 0.7** separates circular-type pores (gas + keyhole) from **lack-of-fusion pores** (form factor 0.3–0.7), while features with form factor **≤ 0.3** or aspect ratio **> 5** are classified as **cracks** (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037). Gas pores are further distinguished from keyhole pores by bluntness (≥ 0.65 for gas, < 0.65 for keyhole) and Feret diameter relative to the population mean (pqac-00000036).

### 4.4 Crack Density Measurement for Hot Cracking in LPBF Al Alloys

Crack density in hot-crack-susceptible aluminium alloys (6061-type, 6182, 7075) is quantified as **total crack length divided by the analyzed area** (units: mm/mm² or mm⁻¹). Jaramillo-Isaza et al. measured crack density in LPBF AA6061 from at least **five optical micrographs** per sample in both XY and XZ cross-sections, using **ImageJ 1.8.0** to trace and sum individual crack lengths (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000051). For LPBF EN AW 6182, Riener et al. reported normalized crack densities ranging from **0.55 to 1.38 mm⁻¹** at 400 °C substrate preheating; at the optimal volumetric energy density of 54.17 J/mm³, crack density was approximately three times lower than at 36.93 J/mm³ (pqac-00000047). Crack-free specimens (crack density effectively zero) were achieved only at **500 °C preheating** with optimized scan parameters, producing a fully equiaxed grain structure (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000049).

---

## Summary of Key Numerical Parameters

| Parameter | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| AlSi10Mg single-track powder layer | 40 µm | Aboulkhair et al. (DOI: 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2015.11.016) |

| Hatch spacing (single layer) | 50–120 µm | Aboulkhair et al.; Volpp et al. (DOI: 10.3390/app11073132) |
| EOS M290 beam diameter | ≈100 µm | Manufacturer nominal |
| Concept Laser M2 beam | ≈54 µm | Maddison 2022 thesis |
| Aconity MIDI/MINI beam | ≈70 µm | Maddison 2022 thesis |
| Shielding gas flow speed | 2–4 m/s cross-flow | Reijonen et al. (DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2019.101030) |
| Hot mounting temperature | 150–180 °C | Geels et al. (DOI: 10.1520/mnl46-eb) |
| Hot mounting force | 15–50 kN | Geels et al. (DOI: 10.1520/mnl46-eb) |
| Keller's reagent | 1% HF, 1.5% HCl, 2.5% HNO₃, 95% H₂O; 10–20 s | Geels et al. (DOI: 10.1520/mnl46-eb) |
| Cu etchant (FeCl₃) | 2 g FeCl₃ + 30 mL HCl + 100 mL H₂O | Geels et al. (DOI: 10.1520/mnl46-eb) |
| Archimedes balance readability | 0.1 mg | Brika et al. (DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2019.100929) |
| Archimedes repeats | ≥3–5 | Porrang et al. (DOI: 10.1139/tcsme-2025-0092); Letenneur et al. (DOI: 10.3390/jmmp4040119) |
| Gas pore circularity threshold | C ≥ 0.95 | Ellendt et al. (DOI: 10.3390/app11136086) |

Gas recirculation through filters maintains O₂ below 0.1% (bosio2021laserpowderbed pages 47-49).

### 1.4 Top-Surface Imaging of Single Tracks

After printing, single tracks are imaged from the top using an **optical stereomicroscope** or a **digital optical microscope** at magnifications of approximately **5×–50×** to assess track morphology, continuity, balling, and width. Track width is measured from calibrated top-view images using intensity profiles or line measurements in ImageJ/MATLAB (vallabh2022predictingmeltpool pages 11-15). Higher magnification (50–200×) may be used for detailed surface morphology.

---

## 2. Metallographic Cross-Sectioning

### 2.1 Precision or Abrasive Cut-Off

Specimens (single tracks or printed cubes) are sectioned using a **wet abrasive cut-off saw** with an **SiC bakelite-bond cut-off wheel** and efficient water cooling to prevent thermal damage and recrystallization (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 392-395). For precision sectioning of small LPBF cubes, a precision cut-off machine with thin wheels (≤1 mm) may be used. The cut is made perpendicular to the scan direction (for single-track cross-sections) or along the build direction (for cubes). Feed rate is controlled to minimize deformation; copious water or water-based coolant flows continuously over the wheel.

### 2.2 Hot Compression Mounting

After sectioning, specimens are hot-mounted in a compression press:
- **Mould diameters**: 25, 30, 31.75, 38.1, 40, and 50 mm are commercially available; 25 and 30 mm are most common for small LPBF specimens (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 80-84).
- **Phenolic (Bakelite) resin**: polymerization temperature **150–180 °C**, mounting force **15–50 kN** (approximately **10–30 MPa** depending on mould area) (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 77-80, geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 84-87).
- **Heating/cooling cycle**: at a 25 mm mould, approximately **6 min heating / 3 min cooling** under pressure; at 50 mm, approximately **11 min heating / 4 min cooling** (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 84-87). The mount must be cooled under pressure to approximately **60 °C** to prevent shrinkage gaps (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 77-80).
- **Conductive mounting compounds** (graphite-filled phenolic or copper-filled acrylic such as Probemet) are used when SEM/EBSD analysis is required; graphite-filled phenolic is preferred for SEM to avoid metallic contamination of the specimen surface (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 77-80, mackenzie2005analyticalcharacterizationof pages 34-39).

### 2.3 Grinding and Polishing Sequences

The following table provides complete grinding and polishing schedules for aluminium and copper alloys:

| Alloy / method | Step | Abrasive / cloth | Grit / grain size | Lubricant | Platen / holder speed (rpm) | Force per specimen (N) | Time (min) |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Al alloys — C-42 | PG | SiC paper | P220 | Water | 300 / 150 | 25 | Until plane |
| Al alloys — C-42 | FG1 | SiC paper | P320 | Water | 300 / 150 | 25 | 0.5–1 |
| Al alloys — C-42 | FG2 | SiC paper | P500 | Water | 300 / 150 | 25 | 0.5–1 |
| Al alloys — C-42 | FG3 | SiC paper | P1200 | Water | 150 / 150 | 25 | 0.5–1 |
| Al alloys — C-42 | FG4 | SiC paper | P2400 | Water | 150 / 150 | 25 | 0.5–1 |
| Al alloys — C-42 | P1 | Diamond suspension on napless cloth | 3 µm | Water–oil | 150 / 150 | 25 | 3–4 |
| Al alloys — C-42 | P2 | Diamond suspension on nap cloth | 1 µm | Water–oil | 150 / 150 | 20 | 3–4 |
| Al alloys — C-42 | P3 | Colloidal silica (OPS), contra-rotation | 0.05 µm | Colloidal-silica suspension | 150 / 150 | 15 | 1–2 (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 373-377, geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 146-150) |
| Cu alloys — C-50 | PG | SiC paper | P220 | Water | 300 / 150 | 20 | Until plane |
| Cu alloys — C-50 | FG1 | SiC paper | P320 | Water | 300 / 150 | 20 | 0.5–1 |
| Cu alloys — C-50 | FG2 | Diamond suspension on soft RCD cloth | 9 µm | Alcohol or water | 150 / 150 | 30 | 3–4 |

*Table: Grinding and polishing schedules for LPBF aluminium- and copper-alloy metallographic sections, including abrasives, speeds, loads, and dwell times. Values are adapted from the C-42 and C-50 preparation methods in ASTM MNL46.*

For **aluminium alloys** (Methods C-42/T-42 from ASTM MNL46), the traditional sequence uses SiC papers from P220 through P2400, followed by diamond polishing at 3 µm and 1 µm, and a final **colloidal silica (OPS) polish at 0.04–0.05 µm** for 1–2 minutes in contra-rotation at 150/150 rpm and 15 N per specimen (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 373-377, geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 146-150). Platen speeds are 300/150 rpm for coarse grinding and 150/150 rpm for fine grinding and polishing.

For **copper alloys** (Method C-50), grinding proceeds through SiC P220 and P320 at 300/150 rpm and 20 N, then transitions to diamond at 9 µm and 3 µm. The final step is a **chemical-mechanical polish** using colloidal silica mixed with 1–2 mL 30% H₂O₂ and 1–2 mL 25% ammonia per 96–98 mL silica, which both polishes and lightly etches the surface (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 395-399, geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 399-402).

### 2.4 Etching

**Keller's reagent for Al alloys**: 2 mL HF (40%), 3 mL HCl, 5 mL HNO₃, 190 mL water (per 200 mL total; equivalent to **1 vol% HF, 1.5 vol% HCl, 2.5 vol% HNO₃, 95 vol% H₂O**). Immerse the polished specimen for **10–20 seconds**, then wash immediately in a stream of warm water (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 213-215). The standard 100 mL formulation is 1 mL HF, 1.5 mL HCl, 2.5 mL HNO₃, 95 mL H₂O (tamadon2017developmentofmetallographic pages 3-5, tamadon2017developmentofmetallographic pages 1-3).

**HF safety**: Keller's reagent contains hydrofluoric acid, which causes severe burns and systemic fluoride poisoning on skin contact. The operator must work in a **fume hood**, wear **HF-rated neoprene or nitrile gloves** (not latex), a face shield, and a lab coat. **Calcium gluconate gel (2.5%)** must be immediately available at the workstation for first-aid treatment of any skin exposure.

**Etchants for Cu alloys**: Ferric chloride solutions are standard. Geels (2007) lists Etchant No. 937 (**2 g FeCl₃, 30 mL HCl 32%, 100 mL water**) and No. 938 (**8 g FeCl₃, 25 mL HCl 32%, 100 mL water**), immersed for seconds to a few minutes (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 231-234). Ammonium persulfate (10 g (NH₄)₂S₂O₈ in 90 mL water) is an alternative for revealing grain boundaries in Cu alloys. Iron(III) nitrate solution (10 g Fe(NO₃)₃ in 100 mL water + 100 mL ethanol) may also be used between polishing steps to remove deformation (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 399-402).

### 2.5 Melt-Pool Width, Depth, Height, and Area Measurement (ImageJ/Fiji)

After etching, cross-sections are imaged at **10×–50× magnification** under an optical microscope. In ImageJ/Fiji:
1. **Calibrate** using a scale bar: draw a line across a known distance, enter the real-world length via *Analyze → Set Scale* (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 611-617).
2. **Melt-pool width**: draw a horizontal line tool across the widest point of the melt pool at the substrate surface; *Analyze → Measure* returns the calibrated width.
3. **Melt-pool depth**: draw a vertical line from the substrate surface down to the deepest point of the fusion boundary.
4. **Melt-pool height** (above-surface bead height): measure from the original substrate plane up to the top of the solidified track.
5. **Melt-pool area**: use the *Freehand Selection* tool to trace the entire melt-pool boundary, then *Analyze → Measure* returns the enclosed area (smith2022meltpoolsprocess pages 29-33, geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 624-628).

Measurements should be taken at three or more locations along each track (steady-state region, excluding the first ~1 mm transient) and averaged (smith2022meltpoolsprocess pages 29-33).

---

## 3. Archimedes Density Measurement

### 3.1 Applicable Standards and Apparatus

Archimedes density of small LPBF cubes (typically **5–10 mm side length**) is measured per **ASTM B962** (for sintered/PM parts, including oil-impregnation correction for open porosity) and **ASTM B311** (for parts with <2% porosity) (porrang2026evaluatingdifferentmethods pages 9-13, porrang2026evaluatingdifferentmethods pages 6-9). The apparatus consists of:
- An **analytical balance** with **0.1 mg (0.0001 g) readability**, e.g., Sartorius SECURA 324-1S (letenneur2020laserpowderbed pages 3-6, brika2020influenceofparticle pages 8-12).
- A **density determination kit** (e.g., Sartorius VF4601): a glass beaker filled with liquid sits on a **bridge** over the balance pan; a wire basket or sinker frame is suspended from the balance hook and submerged in the liquid (brika2020influenceofparticle pages 8-12).
- A **thermometer** (±0.1 °C) to record water temperature.

### 3.2 Procedure

1. **Weigh the specimen dry in air** (m_air).
2. **Immerse in distilled water** containing a **wetting agent** (a few drops of surfactant or Agepon to reduce surface tension and promote bubble release) (brika2020influenceofparticle pages 8-12).
3. **Temperature correction**: record the water temperature and use the standard water-density table (e.g., ρ_water = 0.99705 g/cm³ at 25 °C, 0.99820 g/cm³ at 20 °C) to correct the calculation (porrang2026evaluatingdifferentmethods pages 9-13).
4. **Remove air bubbles**: agitate the specimen gently or use an ultrasonic bath for 30–60 s before the immersed weighing. Visible bubbles on the specimen surface must be dislodged with a fine brush or wire.
5. **Weigh the specimen immersed** (m_water).
6. **Calculate density**: ρ_specimen = m_air × ρ_water / (m_air − m_water).
7. **Repeat**: perform at least **3–5 weighings** and average (porrang2026evaluatingdifferentmethods pages 9-13, letenneur2020laserpowderbed pages 3-6).

### 3.3 Open Surface Porosity and Sealing

Surface-connected (open) porosity allows liquid to infiltrate pores, causing the displaced volume to be underestimated, the density overestimated, and the porosity underestimated. ASTM B962 addresses this by **oil impregnation**: the specimen is vacuum-infiltrated with oil before immersion so that the external surface volume is correctly captured (porrang2026evaluatingdifferentmethods pages 9-13, porrang2026evaluatingdifferentmethods pages 6-9). Alternatively, specimens may be sealed with lacquer or paraffin wax before immersion.

### 3.4 Uncertainty and Comparison with Micro-CT/Image Analysis

Measurement uncertainty for Archimedes density of small cubes is typically ±0.05–0.3% relative density for a 5–10 mm specimen, dominated by the air-bubble effect and balance precision. Rough surface topography of as-built LPBF parts can also introduce systematic error (drobner2022theeffectof pages 23-30). Comparison with micro-CT (at ~3–8 µm voxel resolution) and metallographic image analysis generally shows agreement within **1–3% relative density**; for one 316L sample, Archimedes gave 96.12%, metallography 96.30%, and XCT 97.00% (zheng2021defectanalysisof pages 14-17). Micro-CT may miss pores smaller than the voxel size (~5 µm), while Archimedes captures the bulk average but is affected by open porosity; image analysis samples only the sectioned plane (zheng2021defectanalysisof pages 14-17).

---

## 4. Image-Based Porosity and Crack Density on Polished Sections

### 4.1 Stitched Optical Images and Magnification

Polished (unetched) cross-sections are imaged at **50–200× magnification** using a motorized-stage optical microscope. Multiple fields are captured and **stitched** into a large mosaic covering the entire specimen cross-section (typically the full 5–10 mm cube face). This approach ensures that the porosity measurement is representative and captures the spatial distribution of defects.

### 4.2 Thresholding and the Delesse Principle

Images are converted to 8-bit grayscale and binarized using **Otsu's automatic thresholding** method in ImageJ/Fiji, which separates dark pores from the bright metallic matrix by minimizing intra-class variance. The **Delesse principle** (stereological axiom, first stated by Delesse in 1848) holds that the **area fraction of a phase on a random planar section equals its volume fraction** in the material, i.e., A_A = V_V. Thus, the percentage of dark pixels (pore area) in the thresholded image equals the volumetric porosity, provided the section is representative and the pores are randomly distributed.

### 4.3 Pore Circularity Cut-Offs for Defect Classification

The following table summarizes operational morphology criteria for classifying pore types in LPBF:

| Pore type | Circularity, \(C=4\pi A/P^2\) | Morphology | Typical size/location | Formation mechanism | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gas pore | \(C\ge 0.95\) in PoreAnalyzer; alternatively roundness/form factor \(\ge 0.7\), bluntness \(\ge 0.65\), and Feret diameter below the population mean | Small, smooth, nearly spherical | Relatively small; randomly distributed within melt pools | Entrapped shielding or powder gas, or dissolved gas rejected during solidification | Ellendt et al., 2021, DOI: [10.3390/app11136086](https://doi.org/10.3390/app11136086); Li et al., 2024, DOI: [10.3390/ma17061373](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17061373) (li2024simultaneousporedetection pages 7-10, ellendt2021poreanalyzer—anopensourceframework pages 2-4, li2024simultaneousporedetection pages 1-2) |
| Keyhole pore | Roundness/form factor \(\ge 0.7\), bluntness \(<0.65\), and Feret diameter at or above the population mean; circularity alone does not reliably separate it from a gas pore | Nearly circular in 2-D but generally larger or less blunt than a gas pore | Relatively large; commonly associated with the lower part of a deep melt pool | Collapse or instability of a laser-induced vapor cavity | Li et al., 2024, DOI: [10.3390/ma17061373](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17061373) (li2024simultaneousporedetection pages 7-10, li2024simultaneousporedetection pages 1-2) |
| Lack-of-fusion pore | Typically \(0.3<C<0.7\); operationally \(C<0.7\), excluding crack-like features | Irregular, angular, elongated; may contain unmelted particles | Usually larger than gas pores; concentrated between tracks or layers and along melt-pool boundaries | Insufficient energy, inadequate hatch/layer overlap, or incomplete remelting | Ellendt et al., 2021, DOI: [10.3390/app11136086](https://doi.org/10.3390/app11136086); Li et al., 2024, DOI: [10.3390/ma17061373](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17061373) (li2024simultaneousporedetection pages 7-10, ellendt2021poreanalyzer—anopensourceframework pages 2-4, li2024simultaneousporedetection pages 1-2) |
| Crack | Form factor \(\le 0.3\) in Li et al.; alternatively aspect ratio \(>5\) in PoreAnalyzer | Thin, highly elongated, branched or linear feature | Length-dominated rather than area-dominated; often follows grain or melt-pool boundaries | Solidification/hot cracking or stress-assisted fracture; should be measured as crack length per analyzed area rather than treated as ordinary porosity | Ellendt et al., 2021, DOI: [10.3390/app11136086](https://doi.org/10.3390/app11136086); Li et al., 2024, DOI: [10.3390/ma17061373](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17061373) (li2024simultaneousporedetection pages 7-10, ellendt2021poreanalyzer—anopensourceframework pages 2-4) |


*Table: Operational morphology criteria for classifying gas pores, keyhole pores, lack-of-fusion defects, and cracks in polished LPBF sections. Circularity is not sufficient by itself to distinguish gas from keyhole pores, so bluntness, Feret diameter, location, and formation context are also included.*

In the PoreAnalyzer open-source framework, **gas pores** are identified by circularity C ≥ 0.95, where C = 4πA/P² (ellendt2021poreanalyzer—anopensourceframework pages 2-4). In the multi-feature approach of Li et al., a form factor (roundness) threshold of **≥ 0.7** separates circular-type pores (gas + keyhole) from **lack-of-fusion pores** (form factor 0.3–0.7), while features with form factor **≤ 0.3** or aspect ratio **> 5** are classified as **cracks** (li2024simultaneousporedetection pages 7-10, ellendt2021poreanalyzer—anopensourceframework pages 2-4). Gas pores are further distinguished from keyhole pores by bluntness (≥ 0.65 for gas, < 0.65 for keyhole) and Feret diameter relative to the population mean (li2024simultaneousporedetection pages 7-10).

### 4.4 Crack Density Measurement for Hot Cracking in LPBF Al Alloys

Crack density in hot-crack-susceptible aluminium alloys (6061-type, 6182, 7075) is quantified as **total crack length divided by the analyzed area** (units: mm/mm² or mm⁻¹). Jaramillo-Isaza et al. measured crack density in LPBF AA6061 from at least **five optical micrographs** per sample in both XY and XZ cross-sections, using **ImageJ 1.8.0** to trace and sum individual crack lengths (jaramilloisaza2023correlationofenergy pages 7-10). For LPBF EN AW 6182, Riener et al. reported normalized crack densities ranging from **0.55 to 1.38 mm⁻¹** at 400 °C substrate preheating; at the optimal volumetric energy density of 54.17 J/mm³, crack density was approximately three times lower than at 36.93 J/mm³ (riener2022processabilityofhighstrength pages 10-12). Crack-free specimens (crack density effectively zero) were achieved only at **500 °C preheating** with optimized scan parameters, producing a fully equiaxed grain structure (riener2022processabilityofhighstrength pages 10-12, li2024additivemanufacturingof pages 31-34).
