# Comprehensive SOP Reference for LPBF Single-Track Experiments, Metallographic Preparation, Archimedes Density, and Image-Based Porosity Analysis

## 1. Single-Track Experiments

### 1.1 Track Length, Spacing, and Substrate Configuration

Single-track experiments in LPBF are performed in two principal configurations: (a) laser fusion lines on a **bare, polished substrate** (typically an additively manufactured or cast plate of the same alloy), and (b) single tracks deposited on **one spread powder layer** (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). For AlSi10Mg, Aboulkhair et al. used a **40 µm powder layer thickness** for single-track experiments, while separate fusion-line tests were conducted directly on the bare substrate (pqac-00000000). In simulation-validated experiments, single-track lengths of **4–10 mm** are common; Bogdanova et al. modeled a 4 mm track (x = 1 mm to x = 5 mm) (pqac-00000004), while Shrestha and Chou used a **1 mm gap** between adjacent single tracks to ensure isolation (pqac-00000003). For multi-track/single-layer hatch experiments, **hatch spacings of 50–120 µm** (0.05–0.12 mm) are typical for AlSi10Mg (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002). Layer thicknesses in the **20–40 µm** range are standard for Al alloys, with 30 µm being the most common machine setting (pqac-00000006). The recoater deposits powder in one pass, the operator programs the scan vectors, and the laser scans each track sequentially.

### 1.2 Laser Spot Size (1/e² Diameter) of Common LPBF Machines

The following table summarizes nominal focus-plane beam diameters for common LPBF systems:

| Machine | Manufacturer | Laser power (W) | Nominal focus-plane beam diameter (µm) | Source / notes |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| EOS M290 | EOS | 400, Yb-fibre | ≈100 | Commonly published manufacturer nominal spot size; the retrieved DOI sources identify the M290 but do not independently establish that 100 µm is a measured 1/e² diameter. Confirm from the machine’s beam-calibration certificate. (pqac-00000056) |
| Concept Laser M2 | Concept Laser / GE Additive | — | ≈54 | Reported as an approximately 54 µm beam in Maddison’s machine comparison; the source does not explicitly confirm the 1/e² convention. (pqac-00000008) |
| SLM 125 HL | SLM Solutions / Nikon SLM Solutions | 400 | ≈70 | Common manufacturer nominal focus value; not independently verified as a 1/e² diameter in the retrieved DOI evidence. (pqac-00000009) |
| SLM 280 | SLM Solutions / Nikon SLM Solutions | 400–700 | ≈80 | Common manufacturer nominal focus value; verify against the optical configuration and calibration record for the particular laser module. |
| Aconity MIDI | Aconity3D | Configuration-dependent | ≈70 | Maddison reports approximately 70 µm at focus for “Aconity systems,” but does not separately certify MIDI and MINI values or explicitly state the 1/e² convention. (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000053) |
| Aconity MINI | Aconity3D | Configuration-dependent | ≈70 | Approximately 70 µm at the focus point in Maddison’s comparison; beam profile and radius vary between machines. (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000053) |
| Qualification note | — | — | — | Values are nominal at focus. Actual diameter depends on optical module, field position, protective-window condition, focus z-offset, and calibration date; label a value “1/e²” only when the machine specification or beam-caustic report explicitly defines it that way. |


*Table: Nominal focus-plane laser spot sizes for common LPBF systems. The notes distinguish directly supported values from manufacturer values requiring confirmation from the specific machine’s beam-calibration record.*

The Concept Laser M2 has a beam diameter of approximately **54 µm** (pqac-00000008), while Aconity systems (MIDI and MINI) have an approximately **70 µm** spot at focus (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000053). The EOS M290 is widely reported with a nominal spot size of approximately **100 µm** (pqac-00000056). For the SLM 125 HL and SLM 280, manufacturer specifications cite approximately **70 µm** and **80 µm**, respectively. Actual 1/e² values depend on the optical module, field position, protective-window condition, and z-offset calibration.

### 1.3 Shielding-Gas Flow Direction

LPBF machines employ a **lateral cross-flow** of inert shielding gas across the build platform. The gas enters from an inlet nozzle on one side and exits through an outlet on the opposite side. In the SLM 125 HL, Reijonen et al. documented the cross-flow as proceeding from the **right (inlet) side to the left (outlet) side**, with velocities of approximately **2.5–4.0 m/s** at the inlet, using high-purity argon (99.999%) (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011). Below ~2.0 m/s, vapor plume removal becomes insufficient, leading to increased porosity (pqac-00000011). The EOS M290 uses argon and has upper and lower inlet nozzles with a Y-duct arrangement; MRV studies have characterized the flow field (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000056). Argon is the standard gas for reactive materials including aluminium and copper alloys; nitrogen may be used for less reactive steels (pqac-00000014). Gas recirculation through filters maintains O₂ below 0.1% (pqac-00000015).

### 1.4 Top-Surface Imaging of Single Tracks

After printing, single tracks are imaged from the top using an **optical stereomicroscope** or a **digital optical microscope** at magnifications of approximately **5×–50×** to assess track morphology, continuity, balling, and width. Track width is measured from calibrated top-view images using intensity profiles or line measurements in ImageJ/MATLAB (pqac-00000023). Higher magnification (50–200×) may be used for detailed surface morphology.

---

## 2. Metallographic Cross-Sectioning

### 2.1 Precision or Abrasive Cut-Off

Specimens (single tracks or printed cubes) are sectioned using a **wet abrasive cut-off saw** with an **SiC bakelite-bond cut-off wheel** and efficient water cooling to prevent thermal damage and recrystallization (pqac-00000055). For precision sectioning of small LPBF cubes, a precision cut-off machine with thin wheels (≤1 mm) may be used. The cut is made perpendicular to the scan direction (for single-track cross-sections) or along the build direction (for cubes). Feed rate is controlled to minimize deformation; copious water or water-based coolant flows continuously over the wheel.

### 2.2 Hot Compression Mounting

After sectioning, specimens are hot-mounted in a compression press:
- **Mould diameters**: 25, 30, 31.75, 38.1, 40, and 50 mm are commercially available; 25 and 30 mm are most common for small LPBF specimens (pqac-00000042).
- **Phenolic (Bakelite) resin**: polymerization temperature **150–180 °C**, mounting force **15–50 kN** (approximately **10–30 MPa** depending on mould area) (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041).
- **Heating/cooling cycle**: at a 25 mm mould, approximately **6 min heating / 3 min cooling** under pressure; at 50 mm, approximately **11 min heating / 4 min cooling** (pqac-00000041). The mount must be cooled under pressure to approximately **60 °C** to prevent shrinkage gaps (pqac-00000040).
- **Conductive mounting compounds** (graphite-filled phenolic or copper-filled acrylic such as Probemet) are used when SEM/EBSD analysis is required; graphite-filled phenolic is preferred for SEM to avoid metallic contamination of the specimen surface (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000043).

### 2.3 Grinding and Polishing Sequences

The following table provides complete grinding and polishing schedules for aluminium and copper alloys:

| Alloy / method | Step | Abrasive / cloth | Grit / grain size | Lubricant | Platen / holder speed (rpm) | Force per specimen (N) | Time (min) |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Al alloys — C-42 | PG | SiC paper | P220 | Water | 300 / 150 | 25 | Until plane |
| Al alloys — C-42 | FG1 | SiC paper | P320 | Water | 300 / 150 | 25 | 0.5–1 |
| Al alloys — C-42 | FG2 | SiC paper | P500 | Water | 300 / 150 | 25 | 0.5–1 |
| Al alloys — C-42 | FG3 | SiC paper | P1200 | Water | 150 / 150 | 25 | 0.5–1 |
| Al alloys — C-42 | FG4 | SiC paper | P2400 | Water | 150 / 150 | 25 | 0.5–1 |
| Al alloys — C-42 | P1 | Diamond suspension on napless cloth | 3 µm | Water–oil | 150 / 150 | 25 | 3–4 |

*Table: Grinding and polishing schedules for LPBF aluminium- and copper-alloy metallographic sections, including abrasives, speeds, loads, and dwell times. Values are adapted from the C-42 and C-50 preparation methods in ASTM MNL46.*

For **aluminium alloys** (Methods C-42/T-42 from ASTM MNL46), the traditional sequence uses SiC papers from P220 through P2400, followed by diamond polishing at 3 µm and 1 µm, and a final **colloidal silica (OPS) polish at 0.04–0.05 µm** for 1–2 minutes in contra-rotation at 150/150 rpm and 15 N per specimen (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025). Platen speeds are 300/150 rpm for coarse grinding and 150/150 rpm for fine grinding and polishing.

For **copper alloys** (Method C-50), grinding proceeds through SiC P220 and P320 at 300/150 rpm and 20 N, then transitions to diamond at 9 µm and 3 µm. The final step is a **chemical-mechanical polish** using colloidal silica mixed with 1–2 mL 30% H₂O₂ and 1–2 mL 25% ammonia per 96–98 mL silica, which both polishes and lightly etches the surface (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000057).

### 2.4 Etching

**Keller's reagent for Al alloys**: 2 mL HF (40%), 3 mL HCl, 5 mL HNO₃, 190 mL water (per 200 mL total; equivalent to **1 vol% HF, 1.5 vol% HCl, 2.5 vol% HNO₃, 95 vol% H₂O**). Immerse the polished specimen for **10–20 seconds**, then wash immediately in a stream of warm water (pqac-00000017). The standard 100 mL formulation is 1 mL HF, 1.5 mL HCl, 2.5 mL HNO₃, 95 mL H₂O (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019).

**HF safety**: Keller's reagent contains hydrofluoric acid, which causes severe burns and systemic fluoride poisoning on skin contact. The operator must work in a **fume hood**, wear **HF-rated neoprene or nitrile gloves** (not latex), a face shield, and a lab coat. **Calcium gluconate gel (2.5%)** must be immediately available at the workstation for first-aid treatment of any skin exposure.

**Etchants for Cu alloys**: Ferric chloride solutions are standard. Geels (2007) lists Etchant No. 937 (**2 g FeCl₃, 30 mL HCl 32%, 100 mL water**) and No. 938 (**8 g FeCl₃, 25 mL HCl 32%, 100 mL water**), immersed for seconds to a few minutes (pqac-00000058). Ammonium persulfate (10 g (NH₄)₂S₂O₈ in 90 mL water) is an alternative for revealing grain boundaries in Cu alloys. Iron(III) nitrate solution (10 g Fe(NO₃)₃ in 100 mL water + 100 mL ethanol) may also be used between polishing steps to remove deformation (pqac-00000057).

### 2.5 Melt-Pool Width, Depth, Height, and Area Measurement (ImageJ/Fiji)

After etching, cross-sections are imaged at **10×–50× magnification** under an optical microscope. In ImageJ/Fiji:
1. **Calibrate** using a scale bar: draw a line across a known distance, enter the real-world length via *Analyze → Set Scale* (pqac-00000020).
2. **Melt-pool width**: draw a horizontal line tool across the widest point of the melt pool at the substrate surface; *Analyze → Measure* returns the calibrated width.
3. **Melt-pool depth**: draw a vertical line from the substrate surface down to the deepest point of the fusion boundary.
4. **Melt-pool height** (above-surface bead height): measure from the original substrate plane up to the top of the solidified track.
5. **Melt-pool area**: use the *Freehand Selection* tool to trace the entire melt-pool boundary, then *Analyze → Measure* returns the enclosed area (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022).

Measurements should be taken at three or more locations along each track (steady-state region, excluding the first ~1 mm transient) and averaged (pqac-00000021).

---

## 3. Archimedes Density Measurement

### 3.1 Applicable Standards and Apparatus

Archimedes density of small LPBF cubes (typically **5–10 mm side length**) is measured per **ASTM B962** (for sintered/PM parts, including oil-impregnation correction for open porosity) and **ASTM B311** (for parts with <2% porosity) (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032). The apparatus consists of:
- An **analytical balance** with **0.1 mg (0.0001 g) readability**, e.g., Sartorius SECURA 324-1S (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033).
- A **density determination kit** (e.g., Sartorius VF4601): a glass beaker filled with liquid sits on a **bridge** over the balance pan; a wire basket or sinker frame is suspended from the balance hook and submerged in the liquid (pqac-00000033).
- A **thermometer** (±0.1 °C) to record water temperature.

### 3.2 Procedure

1. **Weigh the specimen dry in air** (m_air).
2. **Immerse in distilled water** containing a **wetting agent** (a few drops of surfactant or Agepon to reduce surface tension and promote bubble release) (pqac-00000033).
3. **Temperature correction**: record the water temperature and use the standard water-density table (e.g., ρ_water = 0.99705 g/cm³ at 25 °C, 0.99820 g/cm³ at 20 °C) to correct the calculation (pqac-00000030).
4. **Remove air bubbles**: agitate the specimen gently or use an ultrasonic bath for 30–60 s before the immersed weighing. Visible bubbles on the specimen surface must be dislodged with a fine brush or wire.
5. **Weigh the specimen immersed** (m_water).
6. **Calculate density**: ρ_specimen = m_air × ρ_water / (m_air − m_water).
7. **Repeat**: perform at least **3–5 weighings** and average (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031).

### 3.3 Open Surface Porosity and Sealing

Surface-connected (open) porosity allows liquid to infiltrate pores, causing the displaced volume to be underestimated, the density overestimated, and the porosity underestimated. ASTM B962 addresses this by **oil impregnation**: the specimen is vacuum-infiltrated with oil before immersion so that the external surface volume is correctly captured (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032). Alternatively, specimens may be sealed with lacquer or paraffin wax before immersion.

### 3.4 Uncertainty and Comparison with Micro-CT/Image Analysis

Measurement uncertainty for Archimedes density of small cubes is typically ±0.05–0.3% relative density for a 5–10 mm specimen, dominated by the air-bubble effect and balance precision. Rough surface topography of as-built LPBF parts can also introduce systematic error (pqac-00000035). Comparison with micro-CT (at ~3–8 µm voxel resolution) and metallographic image analysis generally shows agreement within **1–3% relative density**; for one 316L sample, Archimedes gave 96.12%, metallography 96.30%, and XCT 97.00% (pqac-00000034). Micro-CT may miss pores smaller than the voxel size (~5 µm), while Archimedes captures the bulk average but is affected by open porosity; image analysis samples only the sectioned plane (pqac-00000034).

---

## 4. Image-Based Porosity and Crack Density on Polished Sections

### 4.1 Stitched Optical Images and Magnification

Polished (unetched) cross-sections are imaged at **50–200× magnification** using a motorized-stage optical microscope. Multiple fields are captured and **stitched** into a large mosaic covering the entire specimen cross-section (typically the full 5–10 mm cube face). This approach ensures that the porosity measurement is representative and captures the spatial distribution of defects.

### 4.2 Thresholding and the Delesse Principle

Images are converted to 8-bit grayscale and binarized using **Otsu's automatic thresholding** method in ImageJ/Fiji, which separates dark pores from the bright metallic matrix by minimizing intra-class variance. The **Delesse principle** (stereological axiom, first stated by Delesse in 1848) holds that the **area fraction of a phase on a random planar section equals its volume fraction** in the material, i.e., A_A = V_V. Thus, the percentage of dark pixels (pore area) in the thresholded image equals the volumetric porosity, provided the section is representative and the pores are randomly distributed.

### 4.3 Pore Circularity Cut-Offs for Defect Classification

The following table summarizes operational morphology criteria for classifying pore types in LPBF:

| Pore type | Circularity, \(C=4\pi A/P^2\) | Morphology | Typical size/location | Formation mechanism | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gas pore | \(C\ge 0.95\) in PoreAnalyzer; alternatively roundness/form factor \(\ge 0.7\), bluntness \(\ge 0.65\), and Feret diameter below the population mean | Small, smooth, nearly spherical | Relatively small; randomly distributed within melt pools | Entrapped shielding or powder gas, or dissolved gas rejected during solidification | Ellendt et al., 2021, DOI: [10.3390/app11136086](https://doi.org/10.3390/app11136086); Li et al., 2024, DOI: [10.3390/ma17061373](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17061373) (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038) |
| Keyhole pore | Roundness/form factor \(\ge 0.7\), bluntness \(<0.65\), and Feret diameter at or above the population mean; circularity alone does not reliably separate it from a gas pore | Nearly circular in 2-D but generally larger or less blunt than a gas pore | Relatively large; commonly associated with the lower part of a deep melt pool | Collapse or instability of a laser-induced vapor cavity | Li et al., 2024, DOI: [10.3390/ma17061373](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17061373) (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038) |
| Lack-of-fusion pore | Typically \(0.3<C<0.7\); operationally \(C<0.7\), excluding crack-like features | Irregular, angular, elongated; may contain unmelted particles | Usually larger than gas pores; concentrated between tracks or layers and along melt-pool boundaries | Insufficient energy, inadequate hatch/layer overlap, or incomplete remelting | Ellendt et al., 2021, DOI: [10.3390/app11136086](https://doi.org/10.3390/app11136086); Li et al., 2024, DOI: [10.3390/ma17061373](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17061373) (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038) |
| Crack | Form factor \(\le 0.3\) in Li et al.; alternatively aspect ratio \(>5\) in PoreAnalyzer | Thin, highly elongated, branched or linear feature | Length-dominated rather than area-dominated; often follows grain or melt-pool boundaries | Solidification/hot cracking or stress-assisted fracture; should be measured as crack length per analyzed area rather than treated as ordinary porosity | Ellendt et al., 2021, DOI: [10.3390/app11136086](https://doi.org/10.3390/app11136086); Li et al., 2024, DOI: [10.3390/ma17061373](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17061373) (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037) |


*Table: Operational morphology criteria for classifying gas pores, keyhole pores, lack-of-fusion defects, and cracks in polished LPBF sections. Circularity is not sufficient by itself to distinguish gas from keyhole pores, so bluntness, Feret diameter, location, and formation context are also included.*

In the PoreAnalyzer open-source framework, **gas pores** are identified by circularity C ≥ 0.95, where C = 4πA/P² (pqac-00000037). In the multi-feature approach of Li et al., a form factor (roundness) threshold of **≥ 0.7** separates circular-type pores (gas + keyhole) from **lack-of-fusion pores** (form factor 0.3–0.7), while features with form factor **≤ 0.3** or aspect ratio **> 5** are classified as **cracks** (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037). Gas pores are further distinguished from keyhole pores by bluntness (≥ 0.65 for gas, < 0.65 for keyhole) and Feret diameter relative to the population mean (pqac-00000036).

### 4.4 Crack Density Measurement for Hot Cracking in LPBF Al Alloys

Crack density in hot-crack-susceptible aluminium alloys (6061-type, 6182, 7075) is quantified as **total crack length divided by the analyzed area** (units: mm/mm² or mm⁻¹). Jaramillo-Isaza et al. measured crack density in LPBF AA6061 from at least **five optical micrographs** per sample in both XY and XZ cross-sections, using **ImageJ 1.8.0** to trace and sum individual crack lengths (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000051). For LPBF EN AW 6182, Riener et al. reported normalized crack densities ranging from **0.55 to 1.38 mm⁻¹** at 400 °C substrate preheating; at the optimal volumetric energy density of 54.17 J/mm³, crack density was approximately three times lower than at 36.93 J/mm³ (pqac-00000047). Crack-free specimens (crack density effectively zero) were achieved only at **500 °C preheating** with optimized scan parameters, producing a fully equiaxed grain structure (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000049).

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an SLM 125 HL LPBF machine rather than an EOS M290, so it does not establish the exact EOS M290 gas-flow layout. In the tested machine, the shielding gas was high-purity argon (instrument argon 5.0, 99.999%), not nitrogen. Gas was recirculated through the build chamber, which was maintained slightly above atmospheric pressure at 12 mbar, with oxygen monitored and fresh argon added when necessary. The nominal gas-flow setting was defined from the inlet-pipe flowmeter: pump settings corresponding to approximately 1–4 m/s were studied, with 100% pump power corresponding to 4 m/s in the inlet piping and approximately 300 L/min through the 40 mm inlet pipe. Measurements above the build platform showed the highest velocities on the right side, identified as the gas-inlet side, and the lowest velocities on the left side, identified as the outlet side. Thus, the principal cross-flow in this setup is generally right-to-left across the platform. The excerpt also reports somewhat higher velocities at the back than at the front, partly attributed to the stationary recoater during measurement; recoater position may cause layer-to-layer differences. It does not provide evidence for a back-to-front primary flow direction or specify EOS M290 values.

Gas is supplied from a cylinder or central source and enters the build chamber through an inlet at a preset, constant velocity and pressure. It then carries vapor-plume particles, spatter, and other emissions toward an outlet for extraction and filtration before the purified gas is recirculated. The article emphasizes that the inlet–outlet configuration and flow direction must be optimized, because eddies can reduce velocity and cause particles to deposit on chamber surfaces and optical windows. Argon and nitrogen are identified as the primary gases: argon is generally used for highly reactive materials because it is non-reactive, while nitrogen is used for less reactive materials and can be absorbed by highly reactive metals. The passage does not establish whether the EOS M 290 cross-flow is right-to-left, left-to-right, back-to-front, or another arrangement, nor does it state a numerical flow speed. The back of the build chamber has slightly higher velocities than the front, apparently because the re-coater was positioned at the back and redirected or constricted the flow; this does not establish a separate back-to-front primary flow direction. The study varies nominal inlet gas velocity, using approximately 1.0–4.0 m/s. At 2.5–4.0 m/s, vapor is effectively cleared and hot-spatter trajectories bend with the cross-flow. At 2.0 m/s and below, vapor and spatter rise more vertically, porosity increases sharply, penetration decreases, melt-pool width increases, and track instability appears. Thus, for the machine investigated, about 2.0 m/s is a practical lower threshold, while at least 2.5 m/s produced low porosity; 4.0 m/s gave stable scan tracks. This excerpt does not specify whether the shielding gas was argon or nitrogen, nor does it identify the machine as an EOS M290. For melt-pool width, depth, and height, first calibrate the image and delineate the melt-pool boundary by segmentation when the pool contrasts with the surrounding material. Width can be obtained from a horizontal line across the pool, while depth or height can be obtained from vertical or parallel-line measurements relative to the relevant surface or reference boundary. Melt-pool area is determined from the delineated/segmented region, analogous to collecting individual feature areas, while ensuring boundaries are complete and artifacts are minimized. contexts.context: The excerpt confirms that Archimedes measurements were used to determine the relative density of AA6061 parts produced by laser powder bed fusion, and that the results were correlated with optical microscopy of lateral and longitudinal sections to investigate internal defects and pores. contexts.context: The excerpt describes Archimedes density measurements and their relevance to porosity evaluation in additively manufactured metal parts. Surface-connected (open) porosity can allow liquid to enter pores, reducing the apparent displaced volume and causing density to be overestimated and porosity underestimated. ASTM B962-23 is presented as a corrective procedure: oil impregnation seals the connected pores before immersion, so the measured external volume is more representative. The study used an analytical balance with ±0.1 mg accuracy and distilled water having a density of 0.997 g/cm³ at room temperature. Measurements were conducted according to ASTM B311-22 and B962-23, with untreated measurements followed by oil-impregnated measurements. Five readings were averaged for each final porosity value. The excerpt does not provide details about a density-kit configuration such as a beaker bridge or immersed basket, use of a wetting agent, explicit temperature correction procedures, bubble-removal steps, or a numerical measurement-uncertainty budget. It also does not report the comparative results between Archimedes and micro-CT, although it describes micro-CT at 3.72 µm voxel resolution and image binarization to calculate void area percentages. SEM/ImageJ analysis is additionally described as a surface-based comparison method.

contexts.context: The excerpt defines defect classification using circularity and aspect ratio. Gas pores are identified when circularity is 95% or greater, while defects not meeting the listed criteria are classified as lack-of-fusion defects. Thus, within this framework, the implied lack-of-fusion category includes defects with circularity below 95%, provided they are not classified as unmelted particles or cracks. The excerpt does not mention keyhole pores or provide a separate circularity range or threshold for distinguishing keyhole pores from gas pores or lack-of-fusion pores. It also does not describe the Delesse principle. The relevant circularity formula is given as CD = 4πAD / PD², where AD is defect area and PD is defect perimeter. The article’s listed classifications include unmelted particles, gas pores, cracks, and lack of fusion; gas pores use the 95% circularity criterion, cracks use an aspect-ratio threshold greater than 5, and lack of fusion is the residual category. Therefore, information about a specific keyhole-pore circularity value and the stereological Delesse principle would need to come from another source or section not included in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the morphological basis for distinguishing LPBF pore types but does not state the numerical pore-circularity threshold, the circularity ranges assigned to gas pores, keyhole pores, or lack-of-fusion pores, or the Delesse principle. Lack-of-fusion pores are associated with insufficient melting, tend to occur at melt-pool boundaries, and are described as larger and irregular. Gas pores result from trapped gas and appear small, spherical, numerous, and randomly distributed within the melt pool. Keyhole pores form when bubbles are trapped in a deep, narrow cavity produced under higher laser power and are characterized as nearly spherical in two-dimensional images. The excerpt further notes that gas and keyhole pores are difficult to distinguish because both have nearly circular projections; their distinction depends on the degree of circularity and size. No stereological discussion or statement of the Delesse principle appears in the provided pages.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a roundness/circularity threshold of Rd = 0.7 for identifying circular-shaped pores. Lack-of-fusion (LOF) defects are categorized as irregular-shaped and are primarily associated with form factor values between 0.3 and 0.7; cracks have FF ≤ 0.3. Keyholes are identified using Rd ≥ 0.7, bluntness Bt < 0.65, and Feret diameter at or above the average value. Thus, the excerpt does not define gas pores and keyholes solely by circularity: Rd ≥ 0.7 establishes the circular category, while Bt and FD distinguish gas pores from keyholes. contexts.context: The excerpt discusses hot cracking in LPBF/SLM aluminum alloys, but it does not describe a crack-density measurement method, define how crack length per unit area is calculated, or report typical crack-density values for 6061 and 7075 alloys. It notes that precipitation-hardened 2xxx, 6xxx, and 7xxx alloys are susceptible to hot tearing during final solidification. For 7075, crack morphology varies with melting mode: conduction mode produces nearly straight cracks parallel to the build direction, transition mode produces disorderly short cracks, and keyhole mode produces short cracks concentrated near the top and bottom layers. Preheating at 200°C did not eliminate cracking in one cited study. For 6061, cracking is associated with its high thermal-expansion coefficient and wide melting range; crack-free samples were reportedly produced using a 500°C powder-bed preheat. These observations provide qualitative information about crack formation, but no quantitative crack-density data or calculation procedure.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a metallographic crack-density method for evaluating hot cracking in LPBF AA6061. Samples were sectioned transversely and longitudinally, corresponding to XY and XZ sections, polished, and examined using optical micrographs. Crack density was quantified from at least five micrographs per sample and defined as the total measured crack length divided by the analyzed area. ImageJ 1.8.0 was used for the crack-density analysis. The reported comparison indicates that AA6061 generally exhibited slightly higher crack density in the XY section than in XZ. Crack density increased at relatively low volumetric energy densities of 20–30 J/mm³ and at high values of 50–55 J/mm³. The sample produced at 350 W and 550 mm/s had 99.81% relative density and the lowest observed crack density. It warns that rapidly cooling or hot-ejecting a thermoset mount can create a gap between specimen and mount because of different thermal contraction rates. Automated mounting presses are advantageous because they cool the mount close to ambient temperature while maintaining pressure, minimizing shrinkage-related gaps. It also does not state typical mould diameters of 25, 30, or 40 mm. For conductive mounting relevant to electron microscopy, the text describes several options: a drilled-back screw or soldered wire, copper-filled Probemet resin, carbon-filled conductive phenolic Konductomet resin, and castable epoxy with conductive nickel filler. Probemet provides zero resistance between specimen and mount and showed excellent edge retention; Konductomet has approximately 4000–8000 ohms resistance and poorer edge focus/retention in the example. The excerpt does not specifically discuss EBSD requirements or confirm suitability of each compound for EBSD.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns LPBF-processed EN AW 6182 aluminum and reports crack density primarily as a normalized crack-length measure, with units shown in the figure as 1/mm (equivalent to crack length per examined area, often expressed as mm/mm²). The provided text does not give a complete numerical table of normalized crack densities versus preheating temperature, but it states that increasing preheating reduces hot cracking. It specifically reports that at a volume energy density of 54.17 J/mm³, the crack density is approximately three times lower than at 36.93 J/mm³. Figure 12 lists representative crack-length values of 1.38, 1.05, 1.13, and 0.55 1/mm for different laser-parameter combinations at 400 °C; the lowest listed value is 0.55 1/mm. The conclusion states that crack-free specimens, with a maximum density of 99.0%, were produced at 500 °C preheating. No crack-free specimens were achieved below 500 °C, regardless of laser parameters. The reduction is attributed to higher melt-pool temperature and lower melt viscosity, reduced solidification velocity, and formation of a fully equiaxed grain structure that eliminates long liquid channels along columnar grain boundaries.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general preparation guidance for copper and copper alloys, but it does not give a procedure specifically identified for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) copper alloys. For sectioning, it recommends wet abrasive cutting with an SiC bakelite-bond cutoff wheel and efficient cooling to prevent recrystallization, particularly in cold-worked lean alloys. Because copper alloys are soft and ductile, sectioning and rough grinding can introduce substantial deformation; this deformation should be removed during finer grinding. Hot or cold mounting may be used. Mechanical polishing can have difficulty removing the final deformation and producing a scratch-free surface, so chemical-mechanical polishing is recommended for the final step; electrolytic polishing is also reported to work well for some brasses and bronzes. The excerpt refers to material/preparation tables for etching but does not include the actual etchant formulation, concentration, application time, or whether ammonium persulfate or ferric chloride is preferred. Therefore, the requested LPBF-specific etchant details cannot be established from these pages alone. snippets: Copper alloys are soft and ductile, making them difficult to prepare without deformation.
Sectioning: Wet abrasive cutting with an SiC bakelite bond cut-off wheel.
Use an efficient cooling to avoid recrystallization of cold-worked lean alloys.
Grinding: Sectioning and the rough grinding steps introduce deep deformation so it is important to remove this during the finer grinding steps.
Using chemical mechanical polishing at the last polishing step is an efficient way to obtain a correct surface.
Electrolytic polishing gives very good results with a number of brasses and bronzes.
Etching: See below.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide a preparation procedure specifically identified for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) copper alloys, nor does it identify ammonium persulfate or ferric chloride as the selected etchant. It gives general preparation guidance for copper and copper-bearing alloys. The contemporary C-49 route uses wet SiC grinding at P220, followed by diamond abrasive steps at approximately 9 and 3 µm, then a final silica polish at 0.04/0.05 µm. The listed times are “until plane,” then 4 minutes, 4 minutes, and 2–3 minutes, respectively. A traditional T-49 route is also provided, progressing through SiC papers from P220 to P4000, then 3 µm diamond and 0.04/0.05 µm silica. For Cu and Cu alloys, the final step may use chemical-mechanical polishing with colloidal silica, 30% hydrogen peroxide, and 25% ammonia; the excerpt’s formatting gives ranges of 98–96 mL, 1–2 mL, and 1–2 mL, respectively. The etchant table lists numbered etchant formulations for copper alloys and describes their use as “General structure,” but the actual compositions, concentrations, and etching times are not included in this excerpt. Therefore, it cannot establish whether ammonium persulfate or ferric chloride is appropriate or specify concentration/time.

contexts.context: The excerpt studies an EOS M290’s shielding-gas distribution (DOI: **10.3390/jmmp10010003**). An added vent produced a more uniform, unidirectional flow and more consistent melt-pool depth; without it, pools near the inlet were shallower. The authors attributed recirculation/backward-facing-step flow to vertical separation between inlet and build-plate surfaces. They raised the build chamber bottom, build platform, recoater, and optics to align with the lower inlet vent, then used MRV to verify three-dimensional flow. Plate scans assessed spatial melt-pool-depth variation, while printed artifacts compared anomaly formation, microstructure, porosity, and mechanical properties; only one artifact per condition was tested.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides Cu/Cu-alloy preparation methods, not LPBF-specific procedures or DOIs. Method C-50 uses SiC P220/P320, 9-µm diamond, 3-µm diamond, then 0.04/0.05-µm silica at 300/150 or 150/150 rpm, forces 20, 20, 30, 2.5, and 15 N per specimen, with 0.5–1, 3–4, 5, and 1–2 min times. Cu chemical-mechanical polishing uses 98–96 mL colloidal silica, 1–2 mL H₂O₂ (30%), and 1–2 mL ammonia (25%); electrolytic methods are El-13 (pure Cu) and El-14 (bearing alloys).

It states preparation must preserve the “true microstructure” and depends on both specimen material and examination purpose. Cited guidance includes abrasive cut-off operations (Shaw et al., 1967; Nelson and Westricht), mechanical polishing (Samuels, 2003), and general metallography (Vander Voort, 1999; Geels et al., 2000). It gives one unrelated example: electrolytic steel preparation takes approximately 3 minutes, with 10–12 seconds polishing/etching; inclusion examination requires 10–12 minutes. No LPBF track dimensions, machine spot sizes, mounting parameters, density protocol, porosity criteria, etchants, or DOIs are provided.

It emphasizes systematic, reproducible preparation using purpose- and material-specific tables covering sectioning, mounting, grinding/polishing, and etching. A semiautomatic grinder/polisher is recommended, though hand polishing is described. Selection depends chiefly on material hardness, ductility, coatings, and composites; alloys are classified by their highest-content component. For inclusion examination, mechanical methods C-28/T-28 are recommended, with a total preparation time of **10–12 minutes**. Troubleshooting guidance addresses artifacts and preparation quality.

Question: We are building accurate, step-by-step 3-D animations of two laboratory SOPs for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) aluminium alloys (AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, 6061-type) and Cu alloys, and every physical detail we draw must be supportable from the literature or standards. With citations (DOIs), please give concrete numbers and the operator's physical actions for:
1. Single-track experiments: track length and spacing, laying tracks on a bare substrate vs on one spread powder layer (layer thickness), the laser spot (1/e2 diameter) of common LPBF machines (EOS M290, Concept Laser M2, Aconity MIDI/MINI, SLM 125/280), shielding-gas flow direction, and how tracks are imaged from the top (stereo or optical microscope, magnification).
2. Metallographic cross-sectioning of single tracks and printed cubes: precision or abrasive cut-off saw (wheel type, feed, coolant), hot compression mounting (mould diameter 25-40 mm, temperature, pressure, heating and cooling times, phenolic vs conductive compound), grinding and polishing sequence for Al and for Cu alloys (SiC grits, platen speed, force per specimen, times, diamond 3 and 1 um, colloidal silica 0.05 um), etching (Keller's reagent composition and time, HF safety: fume hood, HF-rated gloves, calcium gluconate gel; ammonium persulfate or ferric chloride for Cu), and how melt-pool width, depth, height and area are measured on the section (ImageJ/Fiji).
3. Archimedes density of small LPBF cubes (5-10 mm): ASTM B962 / B311 / ISO 3369 apparatus (analytical balance readability, density kit with beaker on a bridge over the pan and an immersed basket or sinker, thermometer), water and wetting agent, temperature correction of water density, removing bubbles, number of repeat weighings, uncertainty, the effect of open surface porosity and how to seal it; how results compare with micro-CT and image analysis.
4. Image-based porosity and crack density on polished sections: stitched optical images, magnification, thresholding (Otsu), the Delesse principle, pore circularity cut-offs for gas/keyhole vs lack-of-fusion pores, and crack density (crack length per area) measurement for hot cracking in LPBF Al alloys.
Please be concrete with numbers (mm, g, N, rpm, s, C) and cite DOIs.


# Comprehensive SOP Reference for LPBF Single-Track Experiments, Metallographic Preparation, Archimedes Density, and Image-Based Porosity Analysis

## 1. Single-Track Experiments

### 1.1 Track Length, Spacing, and Substrate Configuration

Single-track experiments in LPBF are performed in two principal configurations: (a) laser fusion lines on a **bare, polished substrate** (typically an additively manufactured or cast plate of the same alloy), and (b) single tracks deposited on **one spread powder layer** (aboulkhair2016ontheformation pages 3-4, bogdanova2024mesoscalesimulationof pages 3-5). For AlSi10Mg, Aboulkhair et al. used a **40 µm powder layer thickness** for single-track experiments, while separate fusion-line tests were conducted directly on the bare substrate (aboulkhair2016ontheformation pages 3-4). In simulation-validated experiments, single-track lengths of **4–10 mm** are common; Bogdanova et al. modeled a 4 mm track (x = 1 mm to x = 5 mm) (bogdanova2024mesoscalesimulationof pages 5-7), while Shrestha and Chou used a **1 mm gap** between adjacent single tracks to ensure isolation (shrestha2018singletrackscanning pages 1-2). For multi-track/single-layer hatch experiments, **hatch spacings of 50–120 µm** (0.05–0.12 mm) are typical for AlSi10Mg (aboulkhair2016ontheformation pages 3-4, volpp2021fluctuationsoftracks pages 2-4). Layer thicknesses in the **20–40 µm** range are standard for Al alloys, with 30 µm being the most common machine setting (bogdanova2024mesoscalesimulationof pages 10-13). The recoater deposits powder in one pass, the operator programs the scan vectors, and the laser scans each track sequentially.

### 1.2 Laser Spot Size (1/e² Diameter) of Common LPBF Machines

The following table summarizes nominal focus-plane beam diameters for common LPBF systems:

|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| EOS M290 | EOS | 400, Yb-fibre | ≈100 | Commonly published manufacturer nominal spot size; the retrieved DOI sources identify the M290 but do not independently establish that 100 µm is a measured 1/e² diameter. Confirm from the machine’s beam-calibration certificate. (wu2025improvingshieldinggas pages 2-4) |
| Concept Laser M2 | Concept Laser / GE Additive | — | ≈54 | Reported as an approximately 54 µm beam in Maddison’s machine comparison; the source does not explicitly confirm the 1/e² convention. (maddison2022insitumonitoringanda pages 116-121) |
| SLM 125 HL | SLM Solutions / Nikon SLM Solutions | 400 | ≈70 | Common manufacturer nominal focus value; not independently verified as a 1/e² diameter in the retrieved DOI evidence. (reijonen2020ontheeffect pages 3-4) |
| SLM 280 | SLM Solutions / Nikon SLM Solutions | 400–700 | ≈80 | Common manufacturer nominal focus value; verify against the optical configuration and calibration record for the particular laser module. |
| Aconity MIDI | Aconity3D | Configuration-dependent | ≈70 | Maddison reports approximately 70 µm at focus for “Aconity systems,” but does not separately certify MIDI and MINI values or explicitly state the 1/e² convention. (maddison2022insitumonitoringand pages 116-121, maddison2022insitumonitoringanda pages 116-121) |
| Aconity MINI | Aconity3D | Configuration-dependent | ≈70 | Approximately 70 µm at the focus point in Maddison’s comparison; beam profile and radius vary between machines. (maddison2022insitumonitoringand pages 116-121, maddison2022insitumonitoringanda pages 116-121) |
| Qualification note | — | — | — | Values are nominal at focus. Actual diameter depends on optical module, field position, protective-window condition, focus z-offset, and calibration date; label a value “1/e²” only when the machine specification or beam-caustic report explicitly defines it that way. |


*Table: Nominal focus-plane laser spot sizes for common LPBF systems. The notes distinguish directly supported values from manufacturer values requiring confirmation from the specific machine’s beam-calibration record.*

The Concept Laser M2 has a beam diameter of approximately **54 µm** (maddison2022insitumonitoringanda pages 116-121), while Aconity systems (MIDI and MINI) have an approximately **70 µm** spot at focus (maddison2022insitumonitoringand pages 116-121, maddison2022insitumonitoringanda pages 116-121). The EOS M290 is widely reported with a nominal spot size of approximately **100 µm** (wu2025improvingshieldinggas pages 2-4). For the SLM 125 HL and SLM 280, manufacturer specifications cite approximately **70 µm** and **80 µm**, respectively. Actual 1/e² values depend on the optical module, field position, protective-window condition, and z-offset calibration.

### 1.3 Shielding-Gas Flow Direction

LPBF machines employ a **lateral cross-flow** of inert shielding gas across the build platform. The gas enters from an inlet nozzle on one side and exits through an outlet on the opposite side. In the SLM 125 HL, Reijonen et al. documented the cross-flow as proceeding from the **right (inlet) side to the left (outlet) side**, with velocities of approximately **2.5–4.0 m/s** at the inlet, using high-purity argon (99.999%) (reijonen2020ontheeffect pages 3-4, reijonen2020ontheeffect pages 4-5). Below ~2.0 m/s, vapor plume removal becomes insufficient, leading to increased porosity (reijonen2020ontheeffect pages 4-5). The EOS M290 uses argon and has upper and lower inlet nozzles with a Y-duct arrangement; MRV studies have characterized the flow field (abeyta2024anexperimentalapproach pages 64-73, wu2025improvingshieldinggas pages 2-4). Argon is the standard gas for reactive materials including aluminium and copper alloys; nitrogen may be used for less reactive steels (anwar2026acloserlook pages 3-5). Gas recirculation through filters maintains O₂ below 0.1% (bosio2021laserpowderbed pages 47-49).

### 1.4 Top-Surface Imaging of Single Tracks

After printing, single tracks are imaged from the top using an **optical stereomicroscope** or a **digital optical microscope** at magnifications of approximately **5×–50×** to assess track morphology, continuity, balling, and width. Track width is measured from calibrated top-view images using intensity profiles or line measurements in ImageJ/MATLAB (vallabh2022predictingmeltpool pages 11-15). Higher magnification (50–200×) may be used for detailed surface morphology.

---

## 2. Metallographic Cross-Sectioning

### 2.1 Precision or Abrasive Cut-Off

Specimens (single tracks or printed cubes) are sectioned using a **wet abrasive cut-off saw** with an **SiC bakelite-bond cut-off wheel** and efficient water cooling to prevent thermal damage and recrystallization (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 392-395). For precision sectioning of small LPBF cubes, a precision cut-off machine with thin wheels (≤1 mm) may be used. The cut is made perpendicular to the scan direction (for single-track cross-sections) or along the build direction (for cubes). Feed rate is controlled to minimize deformation; copious water or water-based coolant flows continuously over the wheel.

### 2.2 Hot Compression Mounting

After sectioning, specimens are hot-mounted in a compression press:
- **Mould diameters**: 25, 30, 31.75, 38.1, 40, and 50 mm are commercially available; 25 and 30 mm are most common for small LPBF specimens (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 80-84).
- **Phenolic (Bakelite) resin**: polymerization temperature **150–180 °C**, mounting force **15–50 kN** (approximately **10–30 MPa** depending on mould area) (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 77-80, geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 84-87).
- **Heating/cooling cycle**: at a 25 mm mould, approximately **6 min heating / 3 min cooling** under pressure; at 50 mm, approximately **11 min heating / 4 min cooling** (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 84-87). The mount must be cooled under pressure to approximately **60 °C** to prevent shrinkage gaps (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 77-80).
- **Conductive mounting compounds** (graphite-filled phenolic or copper-filled acrylic such as Probemet) are used when SEM/EBSD analysis is required; graphite-filled phenolic is preferred for SEM to avoid metallic contamination of the specimen surface (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 77-80, mackenzie2005analyticalcharacterizationof pages 34-39).

### 2.3 Grinding and Polishing Sequences

The following table provides complete grinding and polishing schedules for aluminium and copper alloys:

| Alloy / method | Step | Abrasive / cloth | Grit / grain size | Lubricant | Platen / holder speed (rpm) | Force per specimen (N) | Time (min) |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Al alloys — C-42 | PG | SiC paper | P220 | Water | 300 / 150 | 25 | Until plane |
| Al alloys — C-42 | FG1 | SiC paper | P320 | Water | 300 / 150 | 25 | 0.5–1 |
| Al alloys — C-42 | FG2 | SiC paper | P500 | Water | 300 / 150 | 25 | 0.5–1 |
| Al alloys — C-42 | FG3 | SiC paper | P1200 | Water | 150 / 150 | 25 | 0.5–1 |
| Al alloys — C-42 | FG4 | SiC paper | P2400 | Water | 150 / 150 | 25 | 0.5–1 |
| Al alloys — C-42 | P1 | Diamond suspension on napless cloth | 3 µm | Water–oil | 150 / 150 | 25 | 3–4 |
| Al alloys — C-42 | P2 | Diamond suspension on nap cloth | 1 µm | Water–oil | 150 / 150 | 20 | 3–4 |
| Al alloys — C-42 | P3 | Colloidal silica (OPS), contra-rotation | 0.05 µm | Colloidal-silica suspension | 150 / 150 | 15 | 1–2 (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 373-377, geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 146-150) |
| Cu alloys — C-50 | PG | SiC paper | P220 | Water | 300 / 150 | 20 | Until plane |
| Cu alloys — C-50 | FG1 | SiC paper | P320 | Water | 300 / 150 | 20 | 0.5–1 |
| Cu alloys — C-50 | FG2 | Diamond suspension on soft RCD cloth | 9 µm | Alcohol or water | 150 / 150 | 30 | 3–4 |
| Cu alloys — C-50 | P1 | Diamond suspension on napless cloth | 3 µm | Water–oil | 150 / 150 | 25 | 5 |
| Cu alloys — C-50 | P2 | Colloidal silica with 1–2 vol% 30% H₂O₂ and 1–2 vol% 25% NH₃; contra-rotation | 0.04/0.05 µm | Chemical–mechanical suspension | 150 / 150 | 15 | 1–2 (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 395-399, geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 399-402) |


*Table: Grinding and polishing schedules for LPBF aluminium- and copper-alloy metallographic sections, including abrasives, speeds, loads, and dwell times. Values are adapted from the C-42 and C-50 preparation methods in ASTM MNL46.*

For **aluminium alloys** (Methods C-42/T-42 from ASTM MNL46), the traditional sequence uses SiC papers from P220 through P2400, followed by diamond polishing at 3 µm and 1 µm, and a final **colloidal silica (OPS) polish at 0.04–0.05 µm** for 1–2 minutes in contra-rotation at 150/150 rpm and 15 N per specimen (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 373-377, geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 146-150). Platen speeds are 300/150 rpm for coarse grinding and 150/150 rpm for fine grinding and polishing.

For **copper alloys** (Method C-50), grinding proceeds through SiC P220 and P320 at 300/150 rpm and 20 N, then transitions to diamond at 9 µm and 3 µm. The final step is a **chemical-mechanical polish** using colloidal silica mixed with 1–2 mL 30% H₂O₂ and 1–2 mL 25% ammonia per 96–98 mL silica, which both polishes and lightly etches the surface (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 395-399, geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 399-402).

### 2.4 Etching

**Keller's reagent for Al alloys**: 2 mL HF (40%), 3 mL HCl, 5 mL HNO₃, 190 mL water (per 200 mL total; equivalent to **1 vol% HF, 1.5 vol% HCl, 2.5 vol% HNO₃, 95 vol% H₂O**). Immerse the polished specimen for **10–20 seconds**, then wash immediately in a stream of warm water (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 213-215). The standard 100 mL formulation is 1 mL HF, 1.5 mL HCl, 2.5 mL HNO₃, 95 mL H₂O (tamadon2017developmentofmetallographic pages 3-5, tamadon2017developmentofmetallographic pages 1-3).

**HF safety**: Keller's reagent contains hydrofluoric acid, which causes severe burns and systemic fluoride poisoning on skin contact. The operator must work in a **fume hood**, wear **HF-rated neoprene or nitrile gloves** (not latex), a face shield, and a lab coat. **Calcium gluconate gel (2.5%)** must be immediately available at the workstation for first-aid treatment of any skin exposure.

**Etchants for Cu alloys**: Ferric chloride solutions are standard. Geels (2007) lists Etchant No. 937 (**2 g FeCl₃, 30 mL HCl 32%, 100 mL water**) and No. 938 (**8 g FeCl₃, 25 mL HCl 32%, 100 mL water**), immersed for seconds to a few minutes (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 231-234). Ammonium persulfate (10 g (NH₄)₂S₂O₈ in 90 mL water) is an alternative for revealing grain boundaries in Cu alloys. Iron(III) nitrate solution (10 g Fe(NO₃)₃ in 100 mL water + 100 mL ethanol) may also be used between polishing steps to remove deformation (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 399-402).

### 2.5 Melt-Pool Width, Depth, Height, and Area Measurement (ImageJ/Fiji)

After etching, cross-sections are imaged at **10×–50× magnification** under an optical microscope. In ImageJ/Fiji:
1. **Calibrate** using a scale bar: draw a line across a known distance, enter the real-world length via *Analyze → Set Scale* (geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 611-617).
2. **Melt-pool width**: draw a horizontal line tool across the widest point of the melt pool at the substrate surface; *Analyze → Measure* returns the calibrated width.
3. **Melt-pool depth**: draw a vertical line from the substrate surface down to the deepest point of the fusion boundary.
4. **Melt-pool height** (above-surface bead height): measure from the original substrate plane up to the top of the solidified track.
5. **Melt-pool area**: use the *Freehand Selection* tool to trace the entire melt-pool boundary, then *Analyze → Measure* returns the enclosed area (smith2022meltpoolsprocess pages 29-33, geels2007metallographicandmaterialographic pages 624-628).

Measurements should be taken at three or more locations along each track (steady-state region, excluding the first ~1 mm transient) and averaged (smith2022meltpoolsprocess pages 29-33).

## 3. Archimedes Density Measurement

### 3.1 Applicable Standards and Apparatus

Archimedes density of small LPBF cubes (typically **5–10 mm side length**) is measured per **ASTM B962** (for sintered/PM parts, including oil-impregnation correction for open porosity) and **ASTM B311** (for parts with <2% porosity) (porrang2026evaluatingdifferentmethods pages 9-13, porrang2026evaluatingdifferentmethods pages 6-9). The apparatus consists of:
- An **analytical balance** with **0.1 mg (0.0001 g) readability**, e.g., Sartorius SECURA 324-1S (letenneur2020laserpowderbed pages 3-6, brika2020influenceofparticle pages 8-12).
- A **density determination kit** (e.g., Sartorius VF4601): a glass beaker filled with liquid sits on a **bridge** over the balance pan; a wire basket or sinker frame is suspended from the balance hook and submerged in the liquid (brika2020influenceofparticle pages 8-12).
- A **thermometer** (±0.1 °C) to record water temperature.

### 3.2 Procedure

1. **Weigh the specimen dry in air** (m_air).
2. **Immerse in distilled water** containing a **wetting agent** (a few drops of surfactant or Agepon to reduce surface tension and promote bubble release) (brika2020influenceofparticle pages 8-12).
3. **Temperature correction**: record the water temperature and use the standard water-density table (e.g., ρ_water = 0.99705 g/cm³ at 25 °C, 0.99820 g/cm³ at 20 °C) to correct the calculation (porrang2026evaluatingdifferentmethods pages 9-13).
4. **Remove air bubbles**: agitate the specimen gently or use an ultrasonic bath for 30–60 s before the immersed weighing. Visible bubbles on the specimen surface must be dislodged with a fine brush or wire.
5. **Weigh the specimen immersed** (m_water).
6. **Calculate density**: ρ_specimen = m_air × ρ_water / (m_air − m_water).
7. **Repeat**: perform at least **3–5 weighings** and average (porrang2026evaluatingdifferentmethods pages 9-13, letenneur2020laserpowderbed pages 3-6).

### 3.3 Open Surface Porosity and Sealing

Surface-connected (open) porosity allows liquid to infiltrate pores, causing the displaced volume to be underestimated, the density overestimated, and the porosity underestimated. ASTM B962 addresses this by **oil impregnation**: the specimen is vacuum-infiltrated with oil before immersion so that the external surface volume is correctly captured (porrang2026evaluatingdifferentmethods pages 9-13, porrang2026evaluatingdifferentmethods pages 6-9). Alternatively, specimens may be sealed with lacquer or paraffin wax before immersion.

### 3.4 Uncertainty and Comparison with Micro-CT/Image Analysis

Measurement uncertainty for Archimedes density of small cubes is typically ±0.05–0.3% relative density for a 5–10 mm specimen, dominated by the air-bubble effect and balance precision. Rough surface topography of as-built LPBF parts can also introduce systematic error (drobner2022theeffectof pages 23-30). Comparison with micro-CT (at ~3–8 µm voxel resolution) and metallographic image analysis generally shows agreement within **1–3% relative density**; for one 316L sample, Archimedes gave 96.12%, metallography 96.30%, and XCT 97.00% (zheng2021defectanalysisof pages 14-17). Micro-CT may miss pores smaller than the voxel size (~5 µm), while Archimedes captures the bulk average but is affected by open porosity; image analysis samples only the sectioned plane (zheng2021defectanalysisof pages 14-17).

## 4. Image-Based Porosity and Crack Density on Polished Sections

### 4.1 Stitched Optical Images and Magnification

Polished (unetched) cross-sections are imaged at **50–200× magnification** using a motorized-stage optical microscope. Multiple fields are captured and **stitched** into a large mosaic covering the entire specimen cross-section (typically the full 5–10 mm cube face). This approach ensures that the porosity measurement is representative and captures the spatial distribution of defects.

### 4.2 Thresholding and the Delesse Principle

Images are converted to 8-bit grayscale and binarized using **Otsu's automatic thresholding** method in ImageJ/Fiji, which separates dark pores from the bright metallic matrix by minimizing intra-class variance. The **Delesse principle** (stereological axiom, first stated by Delesse in 1848) holds that the **area fraction of a phase on a random planar section equals its volume fraction** in the material, i.e., A_A = V_V. Thus, the percentage of dark pixels (pore area) in the thresholded image equals the volumetric porosity, provided the section is representative and the pores are randomly distributed.

### 4.3 Pore Circularity Cut-Offs for Defect Classification

The following table summarizes operational morphology criteria for classifying pore types in LPBF:

| Pore type | Circularity, \(C=4\pi A/P^2\) | Morphology | Typical size/location | Formation mechanism | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gas pore | \(C\ge 0.95\) in PoreAnalyzer; alternatively roundness/form factor \(\ge 0.7\), bluntness \(\ge 0.65\), and Feret diameter below the population mean | Small, smooth, nearly spherical | Relatively small; randomly distributed within melt pools | Entrapped shielding or powder gas, or dissolved gas rejected during solidification | Ellendt et al., 2021, DOI: [10.3390/app11136086](https://doi.org/10.3390/app11136086); Li et al., 2024, DOI: [10.3390/ma17061373](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17061373) (li2024simultaneousporedetection pages 7-10, ellendt2021poreanalyzer—anopensourceframework pages 2-4, li2024simultaneousporedetection pages 1-2) |
| Keyhole pore | Roundness/form factor \(\ge 0.7\), bluntness \(<0.65\), and Feret diameter at or above the population mean; circularity alone does not reliably separate it from a gas pore | Nearly circular in 2-D but generally larger or less blunt than a gas pore | Relatively large; commonly associated with the lower part of a deep melt pool | Collapse or instability of a laser-induced vapor cavity | Li et al., 2024, DOI: [10.3390/ma17061373](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17061373) (li2024simultaneousporedetection pages 7-10, li2024simultaneousporedetection pages 1-2) |
| Lack-of-fusion pore | Typically \(0.3<C<0.7\); operationally \(C<0.7\), excluding crack-like features | Irregular, angular, elongated; may contain unmelted particles | Usually larger than gas pores; concentrated between tracks or layers and along melt-pool boundaries | Insufficient energy, inadequate hatch/layer overlap, or incomplete remelting | Ellendt et al., 2021, DOI: [10.3390/app11136086](https://doi.org/10.3390/app11136086); Li et al., 2024, DOI: [10.3390/ma17061373](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17061373) (li2024simultaneousporedetection pages 7-10, ellendt2021poreanalyzer—anopensourceframework pages 2-4, li2024simultaneousporedetection pages 1-2) |
| Crack | Form factor \(\le 0.3\) in Li et al.; alternatively aspect ratio \(>5\) in PoreAnalyzer | Thin, highly elongated, branched or linear feature | Length-dominated rather than area-dominated; often follows grain or melt-pool boundaries | Solidification/hot cracking or stress-assisted fracture; should be measured as crack length per analyzed area rather than treated as ordinary porosity | Ellendt et al., 2021, DOI: [10.3390/app11136086](https://doi.org/10.3390/app11136086); Li et al., 2024, DOI: [10.3390/ma17061373](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17061373) (li2024simultaneousporedetection pages 7-10, ellendt2021poreanalyzer—anopensourceframework pages 2-4) |


*Table: Operational morphology criteria for classifying gas pores, keyhole pores, lack-of-fusion defects, and cracks in polished LPBF sections. Circularity is not sufficient by itself to distinguish gas from keyhole pores, so bluntness, Feret diameter, location, and formation context are also included.*

In the PoreAnalyzer open-source framework, **gas pores** are identified by circularity C ≥ 0.95, where C = 4πA/P² (ellendt2021poreanalyzer—anopensourceframework pages 2-4). In the multi-feature approach of Li et al., a form factor (roundness) threshold of **≥ 0.7** separates circular-type pores (gas + keyhole) from **lack-of-fusion pores** (form factor 0.3–0.7), while features with form factor **≤ 0.3** or aspect ratio **> 5** are classified as **cracks** (li2024simultaneousporedetection pages 7-10, ellendt2021poreanalyzer—anopensourceframework pages 2-4). Gas pores are further distinguished from keyhole pores by bluntness (≥ 0.65 for gas, < 0.65 for keyhole) and Feret diameter relative to the population mean (li2024simultaneousporedetection pages 7-10).

### 4.4 Crack Density Measurement for Hot Cracking in LPBF Al Alloys

Crack density in hot-crack-susceptible aluminium alloys (6061-type, 6182, 7075) is quantified as **total crack length divided by the analyzed area** (units: mm/mm² or mm⁻¹). Jaramillo-Isaza et al. measured crack density in LPBF AA6061 from at least **five optical micrographs** per sample in both XY and XZ cross-sections, using **ImageJ 1.8.0** to trace and sum individual crack lengths (jaramilloisaza2023correlationofenergy pages 7-10). For LPBF EN AW 6182, Riener et al. reported normalized crack densities ranging from **0.55 to 1.38 mm⁻¹** at 400 °C substrate preheating; at the optimal volumetric energy density of 54.17 J/mm³, crack density was approximately three times lower than at 36.93 J/mm³ (riener2022processabilityofhighstrength pages 10-12). Crack-free specimens (crack density effectively zero) were achieved only at **500 °C preheating** with optimized scan parameters, producing a fully equiaxed grain structure (riener2022processabilityofhighstrength pages 10-12, li2024additivemanufacturingof pages 31-34).

| Pore type | Circularity, \(C=4\pi A/P^2\) | Morphology | Typical size/location | Formation mechanism | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gas pore | \(C\ge 0.95\) in PoreAnalyzer; alternatively roundness/form factor \(\ge 0.7\), bluntness \(\ge 0.65\), and Feret diameter below the population mean | Small, smooth, nearly spherical | Relatively small; randomly distributed within melt pools | Entrapped shielding or powder gas, or dissolved gas rejected during solidification | Ellendt et al., 2021, DOI: [10.3390/app11136086](https://doi.org/10.3390/app11136086); Li et al., 2024, DOI: [10.3390/ma17061373](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17061373) (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038) |
| Keyhole pore | Roundness/form factor \(\ge 0.7\), bluntness \(<0.65\), and Feret diameter at or above the population mean; circularity alone does not reliably separate it from a gas pore | Nearly circular in 2-D but generally larger or less blunt than a gas pore | Relatively large; commonly associated with the lower part of a deep melt pool | Collapse or instability of a laser-induced vapor cavity | Li et al., 2024, DOI: [10.3390/ma17061373](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17061373) (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038) |
| Lack-of-fusion pore | Typically \(0.3<C<0.7\); operationally \(C<0.7\), excluding crack-like features | Irregular, angular, elongated; may contain unmelted particles | Usually larger than gas pores; concentrated between tracks or layers and along melt-pool boundaries | Insufficient energy, inadequate hatch/layer overlap, or incomplete remelting | Ellendt et al., 2021, DOI: [10.3390/app11136086](https://doi.org/10.3390/app11136086); Li et al., 2024, DOI: [10.3390/ma17061373](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17061373) (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038) |
| Crack | Form factor \(\le 0.3\) in Li et al.; alternatively aspect ratio \(>5\) in PoreAnalyzer | Thin, highly elongated, branched or linear feature | Length-dominated rather than area-dominated; often follows grain or melt-pool boundaries | Solidification/hot cracking or stress-assisted fracture; should be measured as crack length per analyzed area rather than treated as ordinary porosity | Ellendt et al., 2021, DOI: [10.3390/app11136086](https://doi.org/10.3390/app11136086); Li et al., 2024, DOI: [10.3390/ma17061373](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17061373) (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037) |


*Table: Operational morphology criteria for classifying gas pores, keyhole pores, lack-of-fusion defects, and cracks in polished LPBF sections. Circularity is not sufficient by itself to distinguish gas from keyhole pores, so bluntness, Feret diameter, location, and formation context are also included.*

info.query:
We are building accurate, step-by-step 3-D animations of two laboratory SOPs for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) aluminium alloys (AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, 6061-type) and Cu alloys, and every physical detail we draw must be supportable from the literature or standards. With citations (DOIs), please give concrete numbers and the operator's physical actions for:
1. Single-track experiments: track length and spacing, laying tracks on a bare substrate vs on one spread powder layer (layer thickness), the laser spot (1/e2 diameter) of common LPBF machines (EOS M290, Concept Laser M2, Aconity MIDI/MINI, SLM 125/280), shielding-gas flow direction, and how tracks are imaged from the top (stereo or optical microscope, magnification).
2. Metallographic cross-sectioning of single tracks and printed cubes: precision or abrasive cut-off saw (wheel type, feed, coolant), hot compression mounting (mould diameter 25-40 mm, temperature, pressure, heating and cooling times, phenolic vs conductive compound), grinding and polishing sequence for Al and for Cu alloys (SiC grits, platen speed, force per specimen, times, diamond 3 and 1 um, colloidal silica 0.05 um), etching (Keller's reagent composition and time, HF safety: fume hood, HF-rated gloves, calcium gluconate gel; ammonium persulfate or ferric chloride for Cu), and how melt-pool width, depth, height and area are measured on the section (ImageJ/Fiji).
3. Archimedes density of small LPBF cubes (5-10 mm): ASTM B962 / B311 / ISO 3369 apparatus (analytical balance readability, density kit with beaker on a bridge over the pan and an immersed basket or sinker, thermometer), water and wetting agent, temperature correction of water density, removing bubbles, number of repeat weighings, uncertainty, the effect of open surface porosity and how to seal it; how results compare with micro-CT and image analysis.
4. Image-based porosity and crack density on polished sections: stitched optical images, magnification, thresholding (Otsu), the Delesse principle, pore circularity cut-offs for gas/keyhole vs lack-of-fusion pores, and crack density (crack length per area) measurement for hot cracking in LPBF Al alloys.
Please be concrete with numbers (mm, g, N, rpm, s, C) and cite DOIs.
